 We want to roll out `strata` in production. The idea is with strata we will be able to replicate data across region using the same mirror-pipeline we use for git data, simplifying the architecture and allowing local read
  and write of metadata. The candidates are multiple in the future:
  - project metadata (access, etc)
  - trails
  and others.

  There are two
</pasted_content id="11cf">

 paths I see.

- Start with project metadata, rough idea there is for each project create a "hidden" repository that gets replicated everywhere there is a mirrored repo for that project and start switching readers to that.
- A maybe better path, aim to turn regional CCDB into regional aurora dbs populated using strata. The idea there is to look at the regional CCRDBs data, model it as git repos, bit by bit, and gradually switch to strata.

The goal of this session is to figure out a path forward. That's a lot, any clarificatiion question?
Quick look at the workspace first so my questions are grounded in what strata and mirror-pipeline actually do today.

result.output:
# Strata

Strata is a record store that lives inside a Git repository. Many writers can
write at once, offline if they like, and sync through any ordinary Git remote
without locking or retrying, because each writer appends to a log only it owns.
Every clone folds those logs into the same state, and a projection feed keeps an
external read model, such as a SQL database, up to date for fast queries. Old
data can be compacted, expired or erased on purpose, so a store stays small and
can forget what it has to. Use it to keep application state (plans, mirrored
issues, CI results, document history) versioned and replicated in Git,
with no server of its own and no dependencies beyond the standard library and the
`git` binary.

To see the whole system in one pass, read the
[visual data-flow guide](docs/data-flow.html).

## Records and merge classes

A store holds typed records. Each type picks one of three merge classes:

- **Mutable record**: truth lives in Git; the last writer wins per field.
- **Mirrored record**: truth lives upstream (GitHub, Linear, …); the upstream
  version token decides.
- **Immutable fact**: an observation written once; it cannot conflict.

Merges select a value and never combine two, so counters and collaborative text
belong above the store. The [yjs example](examples/yjs) shows how.

## How it works

A write becomes one commit on the writer's own ref,
`refs/strata/<store>/log/<writer>/<rotation>`. `Sync` pushes those refs (always a
fast-forward) and fetches everyone else's. A read loads the newest *generation*,
a compacted fold of the logs, and folds the live log tail on top of it.

Maintenance keeps the tail short and the repository bounded:

- **Compact** publishes a new generation below the point every writer has passed.
- **Prune** drops log entries that a generation already accounts for.
- **Retain** deletes old generations.
- **Expire** and **Erase** remove facts by age or by name.
- **Evict** and **Retire** release writers that are gone for good.

## Running it

```
mise run check      # format, vet, race, and the property suite
mise run sweep      # concurrency and convergence at higher clone counts
mise run gates      # performance gates
mise run editor     # two browser windows editing one document
go run -C examples ./cmd/strata    # the operator CLI
```

The library has no dependencies outside the standard library. The one exception
is `project/projecttest`, the generated projection properties, which brings
[Hegel](https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-go) into a test that imports it.
Adapters, the SQLite read model, the CLI and the editor live in the separate
`examples` module.

## Limits

- An absent writer stalls compaction until it returns or someone evicts it.
- Announcing to a store needs connectivity. After that, writers can work offline.
- Erased values become unreadable immediately. The bytes are reclaimed only
  after compact, retain, prune and `git gc` have run everywhere.
- History older than the log keeps one revision per generation.
- No adapter has talked to a real upstream yet.

## Further reading

- [docs/design.md](docs/design.md): design rationale, measurements, format
  versioning and the full list of limits.
- [docs/adr/](docs/adr): the decision records.
=====CONTEXT=====
# Record Protocol

A git-native record store. Writers append to their own logs so concurrent writes
never contend, the logs fold into compacted generations so neither clone size nor
read cost grows without bound, and a feed carries changes out to external
projections.

The core vocabulary is inherited from `records-wal-db/CONTEXT.md` deliberately:
two attempts at one problem in one organisation should not speak two dialects.
Terms marked *(new here)* are additions this protocol needs.

## The data

**Store**:
A named collection of Records held in one Git repository.
_Avoid_: Database, namespace

**Record**:
A type and an id, together with the fields currently bound to it.
_Avoid_: Row, entity, document

**Type**:
A namespace string that groups records. It carries no schema and implies no
validation.
_Avoid_: Table, class, kind

**Partition**:
A group of one Type's records, named by a leading run of the segments of their
ids. How many segments a Type divides on is a setting every clone shares, since it
decides where a record sits inside a generation. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Shard, bucket, collection, prefix

**Field**:
One named value on a record.
_Avoid_: Property, attribute, column

**Delete floor**:
The Stamp below which a record has no fields, raised by a delete that names no
field. A floor rather than an erasure: a write stamped above it is visible again.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Tombstone, low-water mark (that word is a Writer's)

**Value bytes**:
The payload a writer bound to a field, byte-for-byte. The protocol selects among
values, bundles them and discards them, but never re-encodes one. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Content, blob, data

## Merge classes

**Merge class**:
Which of three rules a Type's ops fold by. Carried on the op kind, so the fold
needs no schema and no registry. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Strategy, policy, mode, semantics

**Mutable record**:
The class whose fields are authored here and resolve last-writer-wins by stamp.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Local, native, owned

**Mirrored record**:
The class whose value is one opaque payload replicated from an upstream system of
record, ordered by a version token rather than by a stamp. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Mirrored snapshot, cache, replica, sync record

**Immutable fact**:
The class whose records are written once and never revised, so two writers of one
id necessarily agree. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Event, observation, measurement

**Version token**:
An opaque comparable supplied by a use case, expressing which of two mirrored
payloads is more recent. Compared, never interpreted. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Timestamp, etag, revision, upstream clock

**Sidecar**:
A mutable record whose id is a mirrored record's id, holding what we say locally
about data we do not own. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Annotation, overlay, extension, decoration

## Writing

**Op**:
One stamped mutation of one field of one record. The unit of writing.
_Avoid_: Event, commit, mutation, entry (that word is a Log's)

**Writer**:
An identity that owns exactly one log.
_Avoid_: Client, process, user, replica

**Durable writer**:
A writer that appends over its whole lifetime, and whose absence stalls the
barrier until it is evicted. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Long-lived writer, persistent writer

**One-shot writer**:
A writer that creates its log, writes once, never appends, and evicts itself on
completion. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Ephemeral writer, transient writer, job writer

**Announce**:
Publishing a writer's Announcement, which is what makes it a member the barrier
waits for. Required before its first op. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Register, join, enrol

**Announcement**:
The ref a writer publishes on Announcing, holding the Low-water mark it promised
then. It seeds the low-water mark and never moves afterwards: what raises it later
is the writer's Log. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Head, floor (that word is a delete's), registration, membership record

**Prepare**:
Making a repository into a Store this clone may write to: creating the repository
if it is not one, wiring the remote, making writes crash-safe, and Announcing. The
only operation that configures anything — opening a Store to read it leaves the
repository as it found it, so a Projection is never what reconfigures the thing it
is reading. Idempotent, and it Announces only where there is a remote to announce
against. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Init, setup, bootstrap, create

**Log**:
One writer's append-only sequence of ops. Every writer has exactly one, and no
writer ever appends to another's.
_Avoid_: WAL when precision matters — the write-ahead log is all logs together

**Entry**:
One commit on a Log: the Ops a writer wrote together, and the Entry marks that
carry everything before them. Ops are the unit of writing; the Entry is the unit of
appending. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Batch (that word is a Projection's), transaction, commit

**Draft**:
The Ops a writer is gathering for one Entry, which become an Entry when it
commits and nothing before then. Its size is what decides how much one append
costs, since every Entry is a commit. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Session (Entire's own word for a captured AI session), batch,
transaction

**Rotation**:
A successive incarnation of a writer's log ref, incremented when the entries a
generation has already folded are dropped.
_Avoid_: Version, epoch, generation (that word means something else here)

## Ordering

**Stamp**:
The total order key of an op: a Lamport value, the writer that emitted it, and
that writer's sequence number.
_Avoid_: Timestamp, clock, version, revision

**Lamport value**:
The ordering component of a stamp, advanced past everything a writer has
observed. It expresses observation, not time.
_Avoid_: Time, timestamp, tick

**Low-water mark**:
A writer's promise that it will never again emit an op below a given stamp. Its
Announcement states it first and its Log's Entry marks raise it, so the one in
force is the higher of the announced value and one past the highest Lamport Entry
mark the barrier can see.
_Avoid_: Watermark, floor (that word is a delete's), checkpoint

**Barrier**:
The lowest low-water mark across all writers still counted. The point below which
no further op can ever arrive, and therefore the point below which history can be
forgotten safely.
_Avoid_: High-water mark, horizon, frontier

## Reading and folding

**Survey**:
What this clone can currently see of a Store: every announced Writer, every
Log tip, every Eviction and every published Generation, under the Published ref
prefix and among its Tracking refs, enumerated once and then asked. The Barrier,
the Tail, the depth of the Strata and the Erasures in force are its answers, not
things a caller works out from it. Taken fresh per operation and never recorded, since
membership is deliberately unrecorded. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: View (that word is on a Projection's list), snapshot, scan, census

**Follower**:
A clone of a Store that reads and never writes: the Load family, History, the
Feed, Erasures and Status, over whatever can answer for a repository's objects
and refs. It keeps an identity it never publishes, because reads advance a
clock, and it is told its shape by the newest Generation rather than by a
Settings value, since it has no use case of its own. A Store is a Follower with
the write verbs around it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Reader (that word is git's half), Projector (that word is what runs a
Projection), subscriber, consumer, mirror

**Tail**:
Every op the Logs still hold, folded over the newest Generation on every Load.
Exactly the ops that Generation has not folded once every Writer has pruned;
before then it also carries ops the Generation already accounts for, which the
fold absorbs because it is idempotent.
_Avoid_: Backlog, pending, uncommitted

**Generation**:
A published, immutable fold of the log up to a Boundary.
_Avoid_: Snapshot, checkpoint (Entire's own word for a captured AI session)

**Boundary**:
The Lamport value a Generation folds up to: generation n's is n × Step. A
function of the number alone, so two clones that publish generation n fold the
same Ops into it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Horizon, frontier, epoch

**Step**:
The distance between consecutive Boundaries. A Setting, since it decides which
Ops each Generation holds. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Interval, period, granularity

**Strata**:
Every published Generation the store still holds, taken together. Laid down in
numbered order, each folded from the one beneath it, and thinned from the bottom
by Retention. A Load reads the newest layer plus the Tail above it, which is why
the collective needs a name of its own: the depth of the strata is what a
History can reach back through, and what Retention decides. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Layers, stack, history, archive

**Fold**:
Deriving record state from a generation plus a sequence of ops. Deterministic:
the same inputs always produce the same bytes.
_Avoid_: Replay, merge, materialise, project

**Load**:
Reading current record state out of the store: a generation, plus the tail folded
over it. It can be narrowed to some Types, or to one Partition of them, in which
case the generation is read that narrowly — the tail is one stream and is read
whole whatever is wanted of it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Query, fetch, get

**Narrowing**:
What a Load asked for, as a question the Layout scheme can answer: which Types,
which Partition of them, which run of an ordered Type's ids, and whether only the
greatest of those is wanted. One that exists is one the layout can answer, because
the only way to make one is to ask the layout and be refused — so a read that the
shape cannot address is refused where it is asked for rather than quietly widened.
One statement of it decides both which subtrees a Generation is read at and which
of the Tail's Ops belong, which is what stops the two halves of one Load
disagreeing about what was asked. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Filter, selector, scope, predicate

**Revision**:
One value a mutable Field held, with the Generation it was current at. Complete
in the Tail and one-per-Generation below it, since a Generation records what was
current at its boundary rather than how it got there. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Version, snapshot, history entry

**Undo**:
Restoring an earlier Revision by writing it again. It is an ordinary op with a new
Stamp, never a rewrite: the change and its reversal are both in the history.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Revert, rollback, restore

**Conflict**:
Two ops that each believed they were overwriting the same stamp, or two ops of
different merge classes on one record. One wins by ordering; the loser is
recorded.
_Avoid_: Collision, race

**Projection**:
An external read model derived from the feed, holding the deciding stamp beside
each value so it converges without waiting for the barrier. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: View, cache, materialised view, read side

**Feed**:
The ordered stream of ops a projection consumes, resumable from a per-writer
cursor. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Stream, changelog, outbox, CDC

**Since**:
Where a read of a store stopped, in the repository's terms: the commit each
generation and each writer's newest log named, and the erasures in force. A Follower handed one reads on while
holding only what was written after it; anything that publishes a generation,
rotates a log or deletes a ref makes the next read whole. Kept beside the
cursor, not in it: the cursor is how far a Projection has consumed, the same
over any transport, and this is git's. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Checkpoint, watermark, position

**Projector**:
A Projection together with the loop that drives it: read its cursor, read the
Feed from there, apply, and again. Named apart from the Projection because the
mistake it is tested for is not in applying a batch but in when the batch was
read. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Follower (that word is the Store's read half), consumer, subscriber,
worker

## Access

**Identity**:
Who a server has decided is pushing. Set by whatever authenticates the connection
and never taken from the push itself, which is the thing being authorized.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: User, account, principal, author

**Policy**:
Which refs an Identity may move, and in which direction: into existence, out of
it, or from one value to another. Read by the server at receive time, from the
server's own disk, and never consulted by a store. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Permissions, ACL, ruleset

**Grant**:
The set of ref patterns one Identity needs to act as one Writer in one Store: its
logs, its Announcement, its own eviction, and the Store's generations. Derived
from the Ref layout rather than written down, because a Grant that names the
kinds of ref itself is a copy that can fall behind one — and did, omitting the
eviction for as long as the two were separate. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Role, scope, capability

**One-shot grant**:
What an Identity needs to introduce One-shot writers into a Store: create a
Writer's Announcement, its Log at rotation zero, and its Eviction, all together
and all as creations. It names a shape rather than a Writer, because a One-shot
writer's identity is minted as it commits and nothing can name it in advance. A
Writer admitted this way cannot be one that already exists, cannot append
afterwards, and cannot omit its own Eviction. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Ephemeral grant, job grant, runner grant

**Operator grant**:
What an Identity needs to end a Writer that is not itself: create an Eviction for
any Writer, and delete any Writer's Eviction, Announcement and Logs. Broad in
which refs it names and narrow in what it permits — never the direction that moves
a ref from one value to another, because that is the one that would let an
operator speak as somebody else rather than merely end them. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Admin, superuser, root

**Published ref prefix**:
The protocol-owned region of Git refs where Stores publish Logs, Announcements,
Evictions and Generations. Tracking refs and private scratch work use separate
prefixes so they cannot be mistaken for publishable state. Named for what is in
it rather than for the protocol, because Strata is already the name of a Store's
Generations taken together. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Strata ref prefix, namespace, root (that word is one Store's), records
prefix

**Tracking ref**:
A clone's copy of a ref some remote holds, kept under a prefix of its own so a
fetch can never overwrite what this clone publishes. It means what the ref it
tracks means, and no clone ever pushes one. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Mirror (that word is a merge class's), remote ref, fetched copy

**Ref layout**:
Which refs a Store owns and what each one names: a Writer's Logs by Rotation, its
Announcement, its Eviction, the Store's Generations, and its Tracking refs.
One module owns it; it is distinct from the Layout scheme inside a Generation.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Layout, namespace, ref schema

**Layout scheme**:
The structural shape of the tree a Generation's records sit in. Recorded in the
Generation, because a reader that computes a path has to know whether the shape it
assumes is the shape it is reading. One module owns it, and owns the number that
versions it too — the two were five files apart, and the shape changed three times
without the number moving. Nothing to do with the Ref layout. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Format version, schema

**Settings**:
The knobs a Generation's bytes are a pure function of, recorded alongside the
Layout scheme. Distinct from membership, which is deliberately not recorded: these
already decide the bytes, so writing them down adds no way for two compactors to
disagree. A Store is opened with them and they do not change while it is open,
which is what makes "every clone must agree" a fact about a value rather than a
rule about a call sequence. Distinct again from a deployment's own bounds — the
Ceiling and the Ref ceiling — which two clones may set differently without
producing different bytes. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Config, options, parameters

## Housekeeping

The single word "compaction" would cover several different operations, so it
covers only the first.

**Compaction**:
Producing a new generation from the previous one and the tail. The derivation
itself is Shaping, and compaction is not its only caller: Verification runs the
same one over what a Generation recorded about itself.
_Avoid_: Squash, gc, prune, checkpointing

**Shaping**:
The one derivation a Generation's bytes come out of: fold the Tail over the
Generation below, then roll up, erase and expire. Compaction and Verification
both call it, so a published Generation can be rebuilt and compared. The order
of its steps changes no end state and still has to be fixed, because two
compactors that chose differently would publish different bytes for one fold. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Derivation, pipeline, build, compaction (that word is the caller)

**Order width**:
The width, in hex digits, of one level of an ordered Type's record path. A Type
that declares one keeps its ids in its paths, so tree order is id order and a run
of ids can be addressed rather than folded and filtered. Zero leaves the Type
hashed into a shard. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Index, sort key, collation, B-tree

**Verification**:
Rebuilding a published Generation from the one below it and the Ops between their
boundaries, and comparing the bytes. What makes an unsigned Generation
trustworthy, and the reason a Generation records what shaped it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Validation, check (that word is reachability), audit, fsck

**Check**:
Confirming that every ref the Store owns reaches the objects it names, and
reporting each Dangling reference by the ref behind it. Reachability only: a
Check says nothing about whether a Generation's bytes are right, which is
Verification's question. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Verification, fsck, validation, health check

**Roll-up**:
Replacing a closed writer's individual records with one record carrying the same
value bytes verbatim. Extends the Bundle already at its key rather than replacing
it, since a closed writer's records can be folded across more than one Generation.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Coalesce, merge, aggregate, batch, squash

**Bundle**:
The record a roll-up produces: many payloads, each still addressable by the id it
was written under. A Type that rolls up is therefore read at two grains at once —
a Bundle and the loose Facts it replaced can both be present, because Roll-up
removes records from a Generation while a Load folds whatever ops still exist over
it, and the two coexist until Prune. Reading one grain is reading half a Type.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Archive, blob, pack, digest

**Entry mark**:
A high-water value every Entry carries for everything before it on its Log — one
for sequence numbers and one for Lamport values — so Prune cannot lose what the
entries it drops said, and a Writer resuming from its Log cannot reuse a sequence
number or promise below its own past. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Mark alone (it reads as the Low-water mark), watermark, checkpoint,
marker

**Lift**:
Raising a live writer's Low-water mark to everything it has observed, by
appending an Entry with no Ops and a higher Entry mark. Written only when it
would move the Barrier, and never by moving the Announcement, which could reach
a compactor ahead of the Log it vouches for. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Advance, heartbeat, bump, touch

**Prune**:
Dropping the entries of a writer's log a generation has already folded, by
rotating its log ref.
_Avoid_: Compaction, truncate, trim

**Ceiling**:
The tail size past which writes first warn and then refuse. Because a read scans
the tail, the ceiling is the read-cost bound stated as a number.
_Avoid_: Limit, quota, cap

**Ref ceiling**:
The number of live refs past which compaction is overdue. The push-cost bound
stated as a number, since every push pays for every ref. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Ref limit, namespace cap

**Retention**:
Deleting generations older than the ones still needed by readers. Any clone
retains any generation it has seen, fetched or held, and withdraws each from the
remote only while it still holds what that clone saw. The depth is each clone's
own, so the remote is as deep as the shallowest clone that retains. A remote
always keeps its newest generation.
_Avoid_: Expiry, cleanup

**Expiry**:
Dropping records from within a generation because they are older than their
Type's window. A different operation from retention, which drops whole
generations. Expressed to a Projection as a Cutoff rather than a list of what
went, so that removing is stamp-guarded like every other write. *(new here — and
a deliberate divergence from the inherited glossary, which lists this word under
Retention's `_Avoid_`)*
_Avoid_: Retention, TTL, eviction (that word means something else here)

**Cutoff**:
The Boundary a window counted in Generations maps to: for Generation n and a
window of w, the Boundary of Generation n − w. Expiry has one per Type and
Discharge has one per Store, and both are pure functions of n and the Settings.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Bound (that word is an Erasure's), horizon, threshold

**Eviction**:
A recorded op declaring that a writer no longer counts toward the barrier.
_Avoid_: Timeout, expiry, removal

**Retire**:
Deleting an evicted writer's log ref.
_Avoid_: Prune, delete, reap

**Erasure**:
Removing named value bytes on demand, by publishing a Generation without them
rather than by rewriting history. Unlike Expiry it names its target rather than a
window, and unlike Retention it drops values rather than whole Generations. *(new
here)*
_Avoid_: Redaction, deletion, purge, takedown

**Bound**:
The Lamport value an Erasure names, below which a value is gone and at or above
which it is untouched. What makes an Erasure safe to apply twice, and safe to
apply to a value written after it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Cutoff (that word is a window's), threshold, horizon

**Erasure window**:
How many Generations an Erasure is kept for before it Discharges. Counted in
Generations rather than time, for the reason Expiry's window is: two compactors
share the data and not the clock. A Setting, and zero keeps every Erasure for
ever. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Retention (that word drops whole Generations), TTL

**Discharge**:
Dropping an Erasure from the set once its Bound is at or below the Erasure
window's Cutoff. What keeps the erasure set from growing without end. Decided by
the window and never by how many Generations this clone happens to still hold:
Retention is local, and two compactors that consulted it would publish different
bytes for one fold. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Expiry (that word means something else here), retirement, completion

**Dangling reference**:
A ref that resolves to an object this repository does not hold. Not a conflict and
not a merge outcome — a read cannot recover from one, so it is reported and not
retried. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Corruption, broken ref, missing object

**Reconstruct**:
Deriving the whole store from the newest Generation and the Tail above its
boundary, which is all a fresh clone ever has. A routine operation rather than a
recovery procedure. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Restore, repair, import

**Driver**:
What opens repositories, and the seam a caller chooses. A Store is handed one
rather than a directory, so which git drives it is the caller's decision. It
answers for objects, refs and local configuration — never for the wire, which is
a Transport's job and is chosen separately, because the two fail differently: the
primitives a Go git library lacks are all in the ref layer and none of them touch
a push. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Backend, adapter, provider, implementation

**Transport**:
What reaches a remote: publishing refs, withdrawing them, fetching, and listing
what a remote holds. Chosen independently of the Driver, so a clone may keep its
objects through one git and reach its host through another. It writes refs only
by the repository's own mechanism, because two ref-locking protocols over one
repository lose updates silently. What it can promise is a property of the server
rather than of itself, so it is asked per remote and on first contact. *(new
here)*
_Avoid_: Remote, connection, client, wire

**Sink**:
The interface a Projection is written through, whatever database holds it. It is
handed a Batch and a Cursor; it never reads the store itself. It is also handed
each value's Merge class, rather than working it out from the value's shape:
shape only reveals the class while a Record carries one, and two Sinks inferring it separately is how
they came to disagree. An Erasure reaches it as what it named rather than as the
records that went, because once a Generation is published without them the store
no longer holds them to name. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Store, target, backend

# Context Map

Two contexts. The substrate knows nothing about what is stored in it; the
consumers know nothing about how it converges.

## Contexts

- [Record Protocol](./CONTEXT.md) — a git-native record store: writers append to
  their own logs, the logs fold into compacted generations, and a feed carries
  changes out to projections. Lives in the root packages (`stamp/`, `record/`,
  `wire/`, `erasure/`, `orderpath/`, `reflayout/`, `genlayout/`, `settings/`,
  `store/`, `generation/`, `project/`, `authz/`), plus `git/` and `gitbin/` behind them and
  `cmd/strata-receive` in front.
- [Use cases](./examples/adapter/CONTEXT.md) — Planning, Forge mirroring, CI
  observation and collaborative documents. Lives in `examples/`, which is a
  module of its own.

## Relationships

- **Use cases → Protocol**: each use case chooses a **merge class** per Type,
  supplies its own **Id** bytes and (for mirrored Types) its own **version
  token**, and owns its **projection** schema. The dependency is one-way.
- **Protocol → Use cases**: none. The protocol never names a forge, a plan or a
  test run, and its property suite mentions none of them.

  Asserted by `examples/boundary` rather than by the build, since Go allows a

  That test lives on the use-case side because that is where the use cases went
  and it needs both halves in view. The cost is that it protects this
  repository's gate rather than a consumer who vendors the library alone.
- **Authorization** is neither context: `authz/` decides whether a push may move

# Strata: design notes and measurements

Strata is a git-native record store built for a world where many writers work at
once. Each writer gets its own append-only log, so publishing a write is a
fast-forward instead of a fight over one shared branch. Git is both the source of
truth and the transport; projections into an external read model serve fast
application reads.

The name is the shape of the thing. Ops settle into numbered layers, each folded
from the one beneath it; a read takes the newest layer plus the loose material
above it; retention erodes from the bottom. That is not an analogy laid over the
design, it is the design — and forgetting, deliberately and deterministically, is
the requirement everything else had to fit around.

Which is why Yjs was studied closely as prior art and rejected: `Item.origin` is
a *resolved* reference, so no tombstone is ever safe to forget, and a sequence
CRDT is therefore structurally uncompactable. It survives here as an example
sitting *above* the store, where text merge belongs. See the twenty-two records in
`docs/adr/` for that and every other decision a reasonable person would otherwise
re-propose.

If you want the system in one pass, start with the
[visual data-flow guide](data-flow.html). It follows a record from a local
draft into Git, across a remote, through a read and into the maintenance cycle
that compacts, prunes, expires, erases and finally reclaims it.

**Status: all three merge classes work end to end**, each with an adapter that
uses it — planning for mutable records, forge mirroring for mirrored records, CI
observation and collaborative documents for facts. Append, sync, fold, compact,
prune, roll up, expire, erase, evict, retire, retain and project all work across
clones, under a stress sweep at sixteen pressures against four kinds of remote,
including ones that are slow or failing.

## Shape

Two contexts, and the dependency is one-way. The **protocol** knows Store,
Record, Op, Writer, Log, Stamp, Barrier, Generation, Fold, Compaction,
Prune and the projection feed. It does not know what GitHub, Linear, a plan or a
test run is, and an import-boundary test keeps that true. The **use cases** pick
a merge class per type and own their projection schema.

Three merge classes, distinguished by merge rule rather than by byte format, so
they share one envelope, log, transport and compactor:

| Class | Truth lives | Ordered by | Conflict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mutable record | Git | our Stamp | real; last writer wins per field |
| Mirrored record | upstream | upstream's version token | racing syncers only |
| Immutable fact | the observation | nothing — insert-if-absent | impossible by construction |

Each writer owns exactly one log and never appends to another's. That is the
whole of "writers do not contend": every push is a fast-forward, so there is
nothing to lock and nothing to retry.

## How data moves

A write starts as an op and becomes one Git commit on the writer's current log.
The commit uses the empty tree and carries its armoured payload in the commit
message, so an append adds exactly one object no matter how long the log already
is. The ref is the protocol:

```text
Draft.Commit
    │
    ├─ refs/strata/<store>/log/<writer>/<rotation>   append-only log
    ├─ refs/strata/<store>/announced/<writer>        announcement
    └─ .git/strata-<store>.pushqueue                  local publication queue
                         │
                         ▼
                    Git remote
                         │
                         ▼
refs/strata-tracking/<remote>/<store>/*              fetched view
                         │
                         ▼
             newest generation + every live log
                         │
                         ├─ Load: deterministic fold for local reads
                         └─ Feed: resumable batches for projections
```

These names are part of the format, not configurable defaults. Strata owns
`refs/strata/` for published store state, `refs/strata-tracking/` for fetched
copies, and `refs/strata-import/` for private fast-import scratch refs. A
clone's Git config uses `strata.<store>.writer` and `strata.<store>.settings`;
its private lock and publication queue are `.git/strata-<store>.lock` and
`.git/strata-<store>.pushqueue`. “Record” remains the data concept. “Strata” is
the protocol identity on disk.
[ADR-0019](adr/0019-strata-owns-its-git-and-local-prefixes.md) records why the
names are fixed and why fetched refs live in a sibling prefix.

`Sync` pushes local work first and then fetches the remote view. Within the push,
generation refs go before writer refs. That ordering matters: after pruning, a
writer log may no longer contain the ops below a generation's boundary, so the
generation that preserves them must be visible before the shortened log is.
Writer refs and generation refs still travel in separate pushes. Writer refs have
one owner and fast-forward; generation refs are shared, create-only races that the
remote arbitrates.

Reading runs the path in reverse. A clone merges its own refs with the remote
tracking refs, loads the newest generation, then folds the live log tail over it.
Type and partition reads narrow the generation tree; the tail remains one stream
and is always read whole. Re-folding an op already represented in the generation
is harmless. Pruning, not boundary filtering, is what makes the tail cheap.

### The maintenance cycle

These verbs are separate because each one makes a different promise:

| Operation | What changes | What it buys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Compact** | Publishes a parentless, immutable generation below the barrier | A deterministic shortcut for reads |
| **Roll up** | Bundles facts from closed writers inside that generation | Fewer records without changing their value bytes |
| **Expire** | Omits old immutable facts from a new generation | A bounded fact window once older copies are retired |
| **Erase** | Adds a bounded, target-specific instruction to a log entry | Immediate read suppression on every clone that has seen it |
| **Prune** | Rotates this writer's log without ops the generation accounts for | A short tail and fewer commits to fetch |
| **Retain** | Deletes older generation refs, including ones only fetched | Bounded history and objects that Git can reclaim |
| **Evict** | Stops counting an absent writer in the barrier | Compaction can advance, at the cost of that writer returning |
| **Retire** | Deletes an evicted writer's refs after its work is folded | Lower ref-advertisement cost |
| **Git GC** | Removes unreachable objects | Bytes actually leave disk |

Erasure deliberately has two finish lines. The value is **unreadable** as soon as
the erasure reaches a clone, because every load, history read and projection feed
applies it. The old bytes become **unrecoverable** only after compaction writes a
generation without them, retention drops older generations, pruning removes the
source ops, and `git gc --prune=now` runs on every clone and on the remote. A
remote with `receive.autogc` disabled will not do that last step for you.

The [data-flow guide](data-flow.html) turns this lifecycle into diagrams and
links each guarantee back to the code and ADR that owns it.

## Measured

On an M-series laptop, against a bare local remote driven by the real `git`
binary. Reproduce with `mise run gates`.

**A writer's own refs are never refused.** Each clone owns its log outright, so
there is no race to lose.

| concurrent clones | pushes | refused |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | 12 | 0 |
| 4 | 24 | 0 |
| 8 | 48 | 0 |
| 16 | 96 | 0 |

Generations are the exception, and deliberately so. Two compactors can reach one
boundary from different views, so publishing a generation is a create-only race
the remote settles: the loser fetches, adopts what was published, and loses
nothing, because a generation is a shortcut rather than the data. See
`docs/adr/0010`. Writer refs and generation refs are pushed separately for exactly
this reason — sharing an atomic push would let a routine race take a writer's own
work down with it.

**Under sustained concurrency, with compaction and pruning racing the writers**
(`mise run stress`), across three seeds at ten writers for thirty seconds each:

Turned up harder still, `mise run stress-sweep` runs six pressures across four
kinds of remote: one this project configured, one on the `reftable` backend git
3.0 will default to, one somebody else made and left at git's defaults, and one
served over smart HTTP. Only the first was ever tested before, and each of the
other three broke something on its first run.

| remote | what it exercises | what it found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ours, `files` | the configuration we control | — |
| `reftable` | a backend we cannot pin on a remote we do not host | a writer's own push refused: `cannot lock references` |
| unmanaged | `receive.autogc` on, which we require off and cannot set | a push refused mid-object-write, maintenance having pruned the fanout directory under it |
| smart HTTP | the stateless split: advertisement and negotiation as separate requests | nothing in the protocol; a harness that assumed a remote is a path |

Four more points run against a remote that is slow or failing, because latency
and transport faults each had a test of their own and had never had company. A
point with faults asserts something different from the others: a failed push is
expected there, so the writer carries on — its queue is not cleared until a push
is confirmed — and the claim is the one that still has to hold, that nothing is
lost, nothing is invented and every clone agrees at the end. All four pass, and
the split between them is the result:

| point | fault | injected | reached the caller |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `latent-http` | 15ms on every request | — | — |
| `refusing-http` | 1 advertisement in 7 refused | 39 | 39 |
| `unanswering-http` | 1 applied write in 9 unanswered | 13 | 0 |
| `hostile-http` | both, plus 5ms | 34 | 25 |

A refused advertisement always surfaces, and should: the remote did nothing, the
sync did nothing, and a sync that silently did nothing is worse than one that
failed. A write that landed with the answer lost never surfaced once — the push
retries, meets a remote that already has what it is being sent, and finds its own
refs where it wanted them. That is the case a stateless protocol makes real and
the one a retry has to be safe for, and at this scale it is invisible.

The first two are contention rather than disagreement — nothing was decided — so
push retries them, which is a different thing from adopting a rejection. The
distinction matters: a non-fast-forward means somebody else defined that
generation and the answer is to take theirs, while losing a race for a lock or
tripping over a garbage collection means try again.

**A remote can also fail, and that is not the same event as this process dying.**
Every crash injected elsewhere is about what survives a clone stopping; these are
about what survives the far end stopping, which over a stateless protocol it has
two chances to do per operation. The served remote misbehaves to order: refusing
to answer an advertisement, delaying every request, or — the interesting one —
applying a write and then closing the connection without answering.

That last case turned up something worth knowing: **git's own HTTP transport
retries a POST whose connection died**, so a single lost answer never reaches this
code at all. At-least-once is handled below us. Making the caller see a failure
means outlasting that retry, and once it does, the recovery path is the one the
design already relies on — the queue is only cleared after a confirmed push, so
the work is still there, and the retry meets a remote that already holds some of
it. A writer's own refs fast-forward to where they already are; a generation is a
create-if-absent that now finds the ref present, which is the arbitration path
arrived at by a route nobody designed for it.

| | seed 1 | seed 7 | seed 42 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ops | 1,092 | 1,125 | 1,112 |
| generations published | 101 | 99 | 100 |
| prunes | 79 | 87 | 90 |
| ops dropped by pruning | 1,009 | 1,044 | 1,073 |
| push failures | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| fetch failures | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| generation divergences | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Every clone converged, and every value ever written was still readable at the end.

That last clause is the one worth stating, because it was false. Turned up harder
— twelve writers pruning at every opportunity — the suite lost data in four runs
out of thirty: every clone missing the same handful of committed, synced fields,
with no failed push and no divergence to show for it. Pushing a writer's own refs
before its generations left a pruned log on the remote while the generation
licensing the prune was still local, so a clone fetching in that window folded
over ops that no longer existed anywhere and published a generation missing them.
Generations go first now, and the same thirty runs lose nothing. See
`store/prunewindow_test.go`, which crashes between the two pushes on purpose.

The two failure columns used to be one. A refused push would mean two clones
contended for a ref, which this design claims cannot happen; a failed fetch means
a ref was deleted while it was being read, which is routine here — pruning
rotates logs, retention drops generations, retiring removes writers — and git
reports it as `not our ref 000...`, which reads like corruption and is nothing of
the kind. Counting them together made the second look like the first. That one is
retried, narrowly.

**Push cost does not scale with store size.** This was the design's biggest risk:
if publishing one appended op got more expensive as the store grew, splitting refs
per writer would buy nothing.

| records in the store | median push | worst push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 50ms | 53ms |
| 200 | 47ms | 49ms |
| 1,000 | 48ms | 50ms |

**Push cost does scale with ref count, and that is git's, not ours.** There is no
protocol v2 for push, so every push receives an unfiltered advertisement of every
ref on the remote.

| other writers' refs | median push | worst push |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 47ms | 50ms |
| 200 | 68ms | 70ms |
| 800 | 134ms | 138ms |
| 2,000 | 264ms | 270ms |

Roughly linear, which is why evicted writers are retired steadily rather than
left to pile up. Fetch is unaffected, because fetch *can* filter by prefix: reads
scale with ref count and writes do not.

**Compaction bounds clone size, above a threshold.** 100 records rewritten every
round, then compact, prune and `git gc`:

| rewrite rounds | uncompacted | compacted | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | 11 KiB | 30 KiB | larger |
| 20 | 33 KiB | 31 KiB | smaller |
| 60 | 89 KiB | 33 KiB | smaller |
| 150 | 223 KiB | 38 KiB | smaller |
| 400 | 613 KiB | 51 KiB | 12× smaller |

Worth reading both columns. Uncompacted grows linearly; compacted barely moves —
which is the founding claim, demonstrated. But a generation holds one blob per
record, and that layout has a fixed cost, so **below roughly 20 rounds of rewrites
compaction makes a clone larger, not smaller.** Compacting a store that has barely
been written is work for nothing.

Those numbers were taken while every generation ref was kept, which is a lower
bound on the benefit rather than the steady state. Compaction publishes one
generation per boundary crossed and nothing dropped them, so the refs accumulated
and every record blob any generation ever named stayed reachable — `git gc` could
reclaim none of it. `strata retain <n>` keeps the newest *n* and deletes the
rest, which is safe because a later generation folds everything an earlier one
folded. Any clone may retain any generation it has seen, including those it
only fetched, and each withdrawal is leased on the value it saw, so retainers
can race safely (ADR-0026). A store has one remote: its survey reads every
remote it has fetched as one view, so a second remote would let Prune and
Retain act on generations that remote does not hold (ADR-0027). It is also what makes an expiry window real: until the generations
carrying the expired facts are gone, expiry has reclaimed nothing.

**An append is one object, and its cost does not grow with the log.** A log entry
is a commit carrying its ops in its message, against the empty tree — no blob and
no tree of its own.

| log entries | median append | objects in repo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50 | 47.0ms | 54 |
| 350 | 45.6ms | 354 |
| 1,550 | 45.9ms | 1,554 |

Exactly one object per entry, and flat latency across a thirty-fold range. The
~46ms is subprocess spawn cost, which is the floor for driving the git binary.

The earlier layout put ops in a blob and listed every entry in the commit's tree,
so each append rewrote a tree that grew by 61 bytes per entry — quadratic time and
space in the number of appends, and four objects each.

**A generation is streamed into a packfile, not written a blob at a time.**
`git fast-import` takes the whole generation — every record blob, the tree and the
commit — on one pipe in one process, where the earlier path spawned `hash-object`,
`update-index`, `write-tree` and `commit-tree` in turn and left every object loose.
Reproduce with `mise run gen-cost`.

| records | blob at a time | on disk | fast-import | on disk | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1,000 | 691ms | 4.9 MiB | 18ms | 124 KiB | 38× |
| 10,000 | 5.0s | 40.1 MiB | 76ms | 900 KiB | 66× |
| 50,000 | 26.0s | 197.3 MiB | 479ms | 4.1 MiB | 54× |

The disk column is the reason for the time column: a loose object occupies a whole
filesystem allocation block, so 50,000 records of a few hundred bytes each cost
197 MiB to hold 4 MiB of content. The `git gc` that eventually packs them is
superlinear in how many there are — 9.1s against 112ms at 50,000 records, 81×.
After that gc both paths hold the same content in the same space (4.6 vs 4.3 MiB),
which is the point: **the commit is byte-identical either way.** It has to be, or
two compactors on different versions would publish different generations for the
same fold, so a test pins the two paths together over payloads including empty
ones, trailing newlines, NUL and bytes above `0x7f`.

**A generation keeps each type in its own subtree, so a read can fold one.**
`records` holds several kinds of thing and a reader usually wants one of them.
Reproduce with `mise run type-cost`; the tail is pruned first, since a fold reads
it whatever types it wants.

| types in the store | records each | fold all | fold one |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 200 | 34ms | 36ms |
| 8 | 200 | 43ms | 37ms |
| 32 | 200 | 80ms | 45ms |

Modest, and worth being exact about why. Below a handful of types it is slightly
*slower*, because reading two subtrees costs two listings where reading everything
costs one. The gain arrives with variety — about 1.8× at thirty-two types — and is
capped by a fixed cost of roughly 35ms that is git subprocesses rather than
records.

**It does not help a store with many of one thing**, which is the case that
motivated it. Ten thousand documents are ten thousand records of one type, and a
type subtree does not divide them. That needs a level below the type.

**A partition divides one type, and is what makes opening one document cheap.**
A type may declare that the first *n* slash-separated segments of an id name a
partition — `Partition: map[string]int{"doc.update": 1}`, so that `readme/alice/0000000003`
belongs to `readme` — and a generation then gives each partition its own subtree.
`LoadPartition` reads one. Reproduce with `mise run partition-cost`.

| documents | records each | fold the type | fold one document |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | 25 | 45ms | 38ms |
| 100 | 25 | 72ms | 46ms |
| 400 | 25 | 115ms | 41ms |

Folding one document is **flat** — it reads its own 25 records whether the store
holds 500 or 10,000 — while folding the type grows with the store. The 40ms it
sits at is the same fixed subprocess cost that caps the type level; the crossover
is around a thousand records and the gap widens from there without bound.

The number of segments is configuration and not a callback, because a generation's
bytes must be a pure function of the data and of settings every clone shares: two
compactors that disagreed about where a record lives would publish different bytes
for the same fold. A test compacts the same inputs independently on two clones and
compares the generation ids.

**An ordered type keeps its ids in its paths, and the newest one is then a
listing rather than a fold.** Every level of a generation is hashed, which makes
any caller string safe to put in a tree and throws away everything else it said.
For a type whose ids are built to sort — `examples/adapter/doc` numbers a consolidation by its
version and pads it so that sorting the ids sorts the versions — that is the one
property worth keeping. A type may declare an **order width**, and its records are
then laid out at `hex(id) + '+'` cut into chunks of that width, so tree order is id
order and `LoadLast` is the last entry of one listing. Reproduce with
`mise run consolidation-cost`; the tail is pruned first, since a read folds it
whatever it wants of the generation.

| versions | each | fold the partition | read the newest | records read |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 20 | 4 KiB | 40ms | 45ms | 1 against 20 |
| 100 | 4 KiB | 39ms | 42ms | 1 against 100 |
| 400 | 4 KiB | 67ms | 66ms | 1 against 400 |
| 100 | 64 KiB | 53ms | 51ms | 1 against 100 |

# mirror-pipeline

Services that synchronize GitHub repositories into Entire storage, plus the
shared code that binds them to a single protocol contract.

```
                                                        ┌──► cmd/fanout ───────────► NATS mirror_git_v1 ──► cmd/worker ──► entiredb receive-pack
                                                        │      (git-sync routes)      (per region)            │
GitHub webhook ──► cmd/webhook-ingest ──► NATS          ├──► cmd/meta-fanout ───────► NATS github_meta_v1 / github_pr_v1
                     (HMAC verify)        webhooks_github_v1  (display metadata, PRs)
                                                        ├──► cmd/core-fanout ───────► NATS github_push_author_v1
                                                        │      (push authors)
                                                        └──► cmd/trails-fanout ─────► NATS trail_forge_events_v1
                                                               (provider-neutral trail triggers)
```

Each consumer on `webhooks_github_v1` is an independent durable: every one
gets every delivery matching its subject filter, and a message is reclaimed
only when all matching durables have acked it. The worker records terminal
sync failures in a KV failure index;
`cmd/rekicker` re-drives those on a cron cadence.

## Services

- `cmd/webhook-ingest/` — verifies GitHub HMAC and publishes raw forwarded
  webhooks to `webhooks_github_v1`. Stateless; horizontally scalable.
- `cmd/fanout/` — resolves Git mirror routes for `push` events via
  entire-core and publishes target-owned sync jobs onto `mirror_git_v1`
  (cross-region in multi-region mode).
- `cmd/meta-fanout/` — fans out GitHub display metadata (`github_meta`) and
  pull-request (`github_pr`) jobs; also runs the backfill work-queue
  consumers and the resource-lifecycle fan.
- `cmd/core-fanout/` — extracts push authors from `push` events and publishes
  `github_push_author` jobs. Exhausted/malformed deliveries are captured to
  webhooks_github_dlq and Term'd (gated on ENTIRE_WEBHOOK_DLQ_ENABLED, same
  shape as cmd/fanout, pod-crash advisory backstop included).
- `cmd/trails-fanout/` — projects pull-request events (`opened`, `reopened`,
  `ready_for_review`, `closed`, `edited`), branch updates/deletions, and completed check
  suites into provider-neutral, placement-routed `trail_forge` events for
  entire-api. Check-suite refs are forge-reported candidates; entire-api must
  certify the exact ref/SHA against canonical EntireDB state. Our own family's
  suites (gate/status output) are dropped at the border before publishing —
  matched against the stable numeric App IDs in `ENTIRE_INTERNAL_GITHUB_APP_IDS`
  (prod, staging, ...) — so they never enter the per-cell stream and cannot
  re-trigger a gate off our own check run. Event arms land only alongside their
  entire-api handlers: the destination stream is WorkQueue-retained, so
  publishing an unhandled arm early would acknowledge and lose it. Its
  raw-webhook durables retry transient
  failures up to a bounded MaxDeliver and then, on exhaustion, capture the
  delivery to webhooks_github_dlq and Term it (gated on ENTIRE_WEBHOOK_DLQ_ENABLED,
  same as cmd/fanout) so a sustained outage doesn't silently drop trail events;
  malformed input still terminates immediately (captured too).
- `cmd/worker/` — mirror-worker. Consumes mirror jobs, fetches from GitHub,
  pushes refs to entiredb; records terminal failures in the failure index and
  publishes completion events. See `cmd/worker/docs/mirror-sync-guide.md`.
- `cmd/rekicker/` — per-cluster CronJob that re-emits failure-index entries
  so terminally-failed repos are re-driven.
- `cmd/mirror-pipeline-admin/` — operator CLI (webhook redelivery, DLQ
  inspection/replay, failure-index ops, backfill queues). See
  `docs/runbooks/`.

Load-testing tools (local / staging only, not in `.buildkite/deployments.json`):
`cmd/loadgen`, `cmd/mockgithub`, `cmd/loadtest-jetstream` — see
`docs/loadtest-local.md`.

## Shared packages

- `pkg/gitjobs/`, `pkg/metajobs/`, `pkg/prjobs/`, `pkg/pushauthorjobs/`,
  `pkg/trailforgeevents/`, `pkg/donejobs/` — canonical job schemas + typed
  publishers for each stream (publish mechanics shared via
  `internal/natspub`).
- `pkg/webhookevents/` — raw GitHub webhook stream contract
  (`webhooks_github_v1`).
- `pkg/webhookdlq/` — webhook dead-letter capture + advisory backstop.
- `pkg/failindex/` — mirror-sync failure index (KV) shared by worker,
  rekicker, and the admin CLI.
- `pkg/fanoutengine/` — shared NATS-consumer runtime (fetch loop, worker
  pool, Ack/Nak/Term decision tree, DLQ hook) behind the fanout
  binaries.
- `pkg/otelsetup/` — shared OTel tracer/meter setup + baggage plumbing.
  (W3C trace-context propagation over NATS message headers comes from
  go-nuts `natsmsg`.)
- `internal/` — service plumbing: mirror route resolution (`mirrorjobs`),
  cross-region NATS transport (`natsregions`), the shared
  publish core (`natspub`), the health/HTTP runtime (`svchttp`), and build
  identity (`version`).

One Go module at the repo root; dependencies are resolved from `go.mod` and
`go.sum`. Each deployed binary has its own Dockerfile built with the monorepo
root as context.

## CI and deployment

Buildkite owns CI and deployment. `.deploy-authority` is the switch: it reads
`buildkite` today, and `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` and `test.yml` both read
it and skip themselves while it does. The GitHub Actions workflows are kept as
a tested rollback path, not as a second pipeline — see
`docs/runbooks/deploys.md` for how to flip back.

- `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` — runs `.buildkite/verify.sh` on every branch, then
  uploads the deployment graph on main.
- `.buildkite/verify.sh` — installs the pinned toolchain and mints the
  short-lived GitHub credential needed for private Go modules, then runs
  `scripts/ci/verify.sh`.
- `scripts/ci/verify.sh` — build, vet, race tests, gofmt check, lint. Both CI
  systems terminate here, so the checks themselves cannot drift.
- `.buildkite/deploy.py` — renders and runs the per-service graph
  (`staging: <svc>` then `production: <svc>`) from
  `.buildkite/deployments.json`, the single source of truth for the 8 deployed
  services and their images, dockerfiles, and Fleet overlays.

`mise run build|test|lint` runs the same tasks locally that
`scripts/ci/verify.sh` runs in CI.

=====CONTEXT=====
# Record Protocol

A git-native record store. Writers append to their own logs so concurrent writes
never contend, the logs fold into compacted generations so neither clone size nor
read cost grows without bound, and a feed carries changes out to external
projections.

The core vocabulary is inherited from `records-wal-db/CONTEXT.md` deliberately:
two attempts at one problem in one organisation should not speak two dialects.
Terms marked *(new here)* are additions this protocol needs.

## The data

**Store**:
A named collection of Records held in one Git repository.
_Avoid_: Database, namespace

**Record**:
A type and an id, together with the fields currently bound to it.
_Avoid_: Row, entity, document

**Type**:
A namespace string that groups records. It carries no schema and implies no
validation.
_Avoid_: Table, class, kind

**Partition**:
A group of one Type's records, named by a leading run of the segments of their
ids. How many segments a Type divides on is a setting every clone shares, since it
decides where a record sits inside a generation. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Shard, bucket, collection, prefix

**Field**:
One named value on a record.
_Avoid_: Property, attribute, column

**Delete floor**:
The Stamp below which a record has no fields, raised by a delete that names no
field. A floor rather than an erasure: a write stamped above it is visible again.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Tombstone, low-water mark (that word is a Writer's)

**Value bytes**:
The payload a writer bound to a field, byte-for-byte. The protocol selects among
values, bundles them and discards them, but never re-encodes one. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Content, blob, data

## Merge classes

**Merge class**:
Which of three rules a Type's ops fold by. Carried on the op kind, so the fold
needs no schema and no registry. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Strategy, policy, mode, semantics

**Mutable record**:
The class whose fields are authored here and resolve last-writer-wins by stamp.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Local, native, owned

**Mirrored record**:
The class whose value is one opaque payload replicated from an upstream system of
record, ordered by a version token rather than by a stamp. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Mirrored snapshot, cache, replica, sync record

**Immutable fact**:
The class whose records are written once and never revised, so two writers of one
id necessarily agree. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Event, observation, measurement

**Version token**:
An opaque comparable supplied by a use case, expressing which of two mirrored
payloads is more recent. Compared, never interpreted. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Timestamp, etag, revision, upstream clock

**Sidecar**:
A mutable record whose id is a mirrored record's id, holding what we say locally
about data we do not own. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Annotation, overlay, extension, decoration

## Writing

**Op**:
One stamped mutation of one field of one record. The unit of writing.
_Avoid_: Event, commit, mutation, entry (that word is a Log's)

**Writer**:
An identity that owns exactly one log.
_Avoid_: Client, process, user, replica

**Durable writer**:
A writer that appends over its whole lifetime, and whose absence stalls the
barrier until it is evicted. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Long-lived writer, persistent writer

**One-shot writer**:
A writer that creates its log, writes once, never appends, and evicts itself on
completion. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Ephemeral writer, transient writer, job writer

**Announce**:
Publishing a writer's Announcement, which is what makes it a member the barrier
waits for. Required before its first op. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Register, join, enrol

**Announcement**:
The ref a writer publishes on Announcing, holding the Low-water mark it promised
then. It seeds the low-water mark and never moves afterwards: what raises it later
is the writer's Log. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Head, floor (that word is a delete's), registration, membership record

**Prepare**:
Making a repository into a Store this clone may write to: creating the repository
if it is not one, wiring the remote, making writes crash-safe, and Announcing. The
only operation that configures anything — opening a Store to read it leaves the
repository as it found it, so a Projection is never what reconfigures the thing it
is reading. Idempotent, and it Announces only where there is a remote to announce
against. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Init, setup, bootstrap, create

**Log**:
One writer's append-only sequence of ops. Every writer has exactly one, and no
writer ever appends to another's.
_Avoid_: WAL when precision matters — the write-ahead log is all logs together

**Entry**:
One commit on a Log: the Ops a writer wrote together, and the Entry marks that
carry everything before them. Ops are the unit of writing; the Entry is the unit of
appending. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Batch (that word is a Projection's), transaction, commit

**Draft**:
The Ops a writer is gathering for one Entry, which become an Entry when it
commits and nothing before then. Its size is what decides how much one append
costs, since every Entry is a commit. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Session (Entire's own word for a captured AI session), batch,
transaction

**Rotation**:
A successive incarnation of a writer's log ref, incremented when the entries a
generation has already folded are dropped.
_Avoid_: Version, epoch, generation (that word means something else here)

## Ordering

**Stamp**:
The total order key of an op: a Lamport value, the writer that emitted it, and
that writer's sequence number.
_Avoid_: Timestamp, clock, version, revision

**Lamport value**:
The ordering component of a stamp, advanced past everything a writer has
observed. It expresses observation, not time.
_Avoid_: Time, timestamp, tick

**Low-water mark**:
A writer's promise that it will never again emit an op below a given stamp. Its
Announcement states it first and its Log's Entry marks raise it, so the one in
force is the higher of the announced value and one past the highest Lamport Entry
mark the barrier can see.
_Avoid_: Watermark, floor (that word is a delete's), checkpoint

**Barrier**:
The lowest low-water mark across all writers still counted. The point below which
no further op can ever arrive, and therefore the point below which history can be
forgotten safely.
_Avoid_: High-water mark, horizon, frontier

## Reading and folding

**Survey**:
What this clone can currently see of a Store: every announced Writer, every
Log tip, every Eviction and every published Generation, under the Published ref
prefix and among its Tracking refs, enumerated once and then asked. The Barrier,
the Tail, the depth of the Strata and the Erasures in force are its answers, not
things a caller works out from it. Taken fresh per operation and never recorded, since
membership is deliberately unrecorded. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: View (that word is on a Projection's list), snapshot, scan, census

**Follower**:
A clone of a Store that reads and never writes: the Load family, History, the
Feed, Erasures and Status, over whatever can answer for a repository's objects
and refs. It keeps an identity it never publishes, because reads advance a
clock, and it is told its shape by the newest Generation rather than by a
Settings value, since it has no use case of its own. A Store is a Follower with
the write verbs around it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Reader (that word is git's half), Projector (that word is what runs a
Projection), subscriber, consumer, mirror

**Tail**:
Every op the Logs still hold, folded over the newest Generation on every Load.
Exactly the ops that Generation has not folded once every Writer has pruned;
before then it also carries ops the Generation already accounts for, which the
fold absorbs because it is idempotent.
_Avoid_: Backlog, pending, uncommitted

**Generation**:
A published, immutable fold of the log up to a Boundary.
_Avoid_: Snapshot, checkpoint (Entire's own word for a captured AI session)

**Boundary**:
The Lamport value a Generation folds up to: generation n's is n × Step. A
function of the number alone, so two clones that publish generation n fold the
same Ops into it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Horizon, frontier, epoch

**Step**:
The distance between consecutive Boundaries. A Setting, since it decides which
Ops each Generation holds. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Interval, period, granularity

**Strata**:
Every published Generation the store still holds, taken together. Laid down in
numbered order, each folded from the one beneath it, and thinned from the bottom
by Retention. A Load reads the newest layer plus the Tail above it, which is why
the collective needs a name of its own: the depth of the strata is what a
History can reach back through, and what Retention decides. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Layers, stack, history, archive

**Fold**:
Deriving record state from a generation plus a sequence of ops. Deterministic:
the same inputs always produce the same bytes.
_Avoid_: Replay, merge, materialise, project

**Load**:
Reading current record state out of the store: a generation, plus the tail folded
over it. It can be narrowed to some Types, or to one Partition of them, in which
case the generation is read that narrowly — the tail is one stream and is read
whole whatever is wanted of it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Query, fetch, get

**Narrowing**:
What a Load asked for, as a question the Layout scheme can answer: which Types,
which Partition of them, which run of an ordered Type's ids, and whether only the
greatest of those is wanted. One that exists is one the layout can answer, because
the only way to make one is to ask the layout and be refused — so a read that the
shape cannot address is refused where it is asked for rather than quietly widened.
One statement of it decides both which subtrees a Generation is read at and which
of the Tail's Ops belong, which is what stops the two halves of one Load
disagreeing about what was asked. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Filter, selector, scope, predicate

**Revision**:
One value a mutable Field held, with the Generation it was current at. Complete
in the Tail and one-per-Generation below it, since a Generation records what was
current at its boundary rather than how it got there. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Version, snapshot, history entry

**Undo**:
Restoring an earlier Revision by writing it again. It is an ordinary op with a new
Stamp, never a rewrite: the change and its reversal are both in the history.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Revert, rollback, restore

**Conflict**:
Two ops that each believed they were overwriting the same stamp, or two ops of
different merge classes on one record. One wins by ordering; the loser is
recorded.
_Avoid_: Collision, race

**Projection**:
An external read model derived from the feed, holding the deciding stamp beside
each value so it converges without waiting for the barrier. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: View, cache, materialised view, read side

**Feed**:
The ordered stream of ops a projection consumes, resumable from a per-writer
cursor. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Stream, changelog, outbox, CDC

**Since**:
Where a read of a store stopped, in the repository's terms: the commit each
generation and each writer's newest log named, and the erasures in force. A Follower handed one reads on while
holding only what was written after it; anything that publishes a generation,
rotates a log or deletes a ref makes the next read whole. Kept beside the
cursor, not in it: the cursor is how far a Projection has consumed, the same
over any transport, and this is git's. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Checkpoint, watermark, position

**Projector**:
A Projection together with the loop that drives it: read its cursor, read the
Feed from there, apply, and again. Named apart from the Projection because the
mistake it is tested for is not in applying a batch but in when the batch was
read. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Follower (that word is the Store's read half), consumer, subscriber,
worker

## Access

**Identity**:
Who a server has decided is pushing. Set by whatever authenticates the connection
and never taken from the push itself, which is the thing being authorized.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: User, account, principal, author

**Policy**:
Which refs an Identity may move, and in which direction: into existence, out of
it, or from one value to another. Read by the server at receive time, from the
server's own disk, and never consulted by a store. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Permissions, ACL, ruleset

**Grant**:
The set of ref patterns one Identity needs to act as one Writer in one Store: its
logs, its Announcement, its own eviction, and the Store's generations. Derived
from the Ref layout rather than written down, because a Grant that names the
kinds of ref itself is a copy that can fall behind one — and did, omitting the
eviction for as long as the two were separate. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Role, scope, capability

**One-shot grant**:
What an Identity needs to introduce One-shot writers into a Store: create a
Writer's Announcement, its Log at rotation zero, and its Eviction, all together
and all as creations. It names a shape rather than a Writer, because a One-shot
writer's identity is minted as it commits and nothing can name it in advance. A
Writer admitted this way cannot be one that already exists, cannot append
afterwards, and cannot omit its own Eviction. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Ephemeral grant, job grant, runner grant

**Operator grant**:
What an Identity needs to end a Writer that is not itself: create an Eviction for
any Writer, and delete any Writer's Eviction, Announcement and Logs. Broad in
which refs it names and narrow in what it permits — never the direction that moves
a ref from one value to another, because that is the one that would let an
operator speak as somebody else rather than merely end them. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Admin, superuser, root

**Published ref prefix**:
The protocol-owned region of Git refs where Stores publish Logs, Announcements,
Evictions and Generations. Tracking refs and private scratch work use separate
prefixes so they cannot be mistaken for publishable state. Named for what is in
it rather than for the protocol, because Strata is already the name of a Store's
Generations taken together. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Strata ref prefix, namespace, root (that word is one Store's), records
prefix

**Tracking ref**:
A clone's copy of a ref some remote holds, kept under a prefix of its own so a
fetch can never overwrite what this clone publishes. It means what the ref it
tracks means, and no clone ever pushes one. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Mirror (that word is a merge class's), remote ref, fetched copy

**Ref layout**:
Which refs a Store owns and what each one names: a Writer's Logs by Rotation, its
Announcement, its Eviction, the Store's Generations, and its Tracking refs.
One module owns it; it is distinct from the Layout scheme inside a Generation.
*(new here)*
_Avoid_: Layout, namespace, ref schema

**Layout scheme**:
The structural shape of the tree a Generation's records sit in. Recorded in the
Generation, because a reader that computes a path has to know whether the shape it
assumes is the shape it is reading. One module owns it, and owns the number that
versions it too — the two were five files apart, and the shape changed three times
without the number moving. Nothing to do with the Ref layout. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Format version, schema

**Settings**:
The knobs a Generation's bytes are a pure function of, recorded alongside the
Layout scheme. Distinct from membership, which is deliberately not recorded: these
already decide the bytes, so writing them down adds no way for two compactors to
disagree. A Store is opened with them and they do not change while it is open,
which is what makes "every clone must agree" a fact about a value rather than a
rule about a call sequence. Distinct again from a deployment's own bounds — the
Ceiling and the Ref ceiling — which two clones may set differently without
producing different bytes. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Config, options, parameters

## Housekeeping

The single word "compaction" would cover several different operations, so it
covers only the first.

**Compaction**:
Producing a new generation from the previous one and the tail. The derivation
itself is Shaping, and compaction is not its only caller: Verification runs the
same one over what a Generation recorded about itself.
_Avoid_: Squash, gc, prune, checkpointing

**Shaping**:
The one derivation a Generation's bytes come out of: fold the Tail over the
Generation below, then roll up, erase and expire. Compaction and Verification
both call it, so a published Generation can be rebuilt and compared. The order
of its steps changes no end state and still has to be fixed, because two
compactors that chose differently would publish different bytes for one fold. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Derivation, pipeline, build, compaction (that word is the caller)

**Order width**:
The width, in hex digits, of one level of an ordered Type's record path. A Type
that declares one keeps its ids in its paths, so tree order is id order and a run
of ids can be addressed rather than folded and filtered. Zero leaves the Type
hashed into a shard. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Index, sort key, collation, B-tree

**Verification**:
Rebuilding a published Generation from the one below it and the Ops between their
boundaries, and comparing the bytes. What makes an unsigned Generation
trustworthy, and the reason a Generation records what shaped it. *(new here)*
_Avoid_: Validation, check (that word is reachability), audit, fsck

**Check**:
