# entire-api

The product API for a cell: one HTTP surface that serves Entire's domain objects
and fronts the cell's git data plane. It consolidates the former `activity` and
`api-gateway` services into a per-jurisdiction Go module of **three deployable
processes** — two workers and the unified HTTP server — over two PostgreSQL
databases:

- **user-activity** (`cmd/user-activity`) — the user-side worker: runs the
  forwarder consumer that writes the **user store** from inbound
  `user_activity` events. Health probes only.
- **repo-activity** (`cmd/repo-activity`) — the repo-side worker: ingests
  `repo_refs_v1` into the **repo store** and forwards residency-safe metadata to
  authors' home regions. It also runs the **checkpoint-analysis** consumer
  (`analysis-facets` on `repo_checkpoint_analysis_jobs`), deriving each
  checkpoint's recap facets — the deterministic skills/tools half, plus the LLM
  `labels` half (Anthropic API) when `ANALYZE_CHECKPOINTS` is on. On an Anthropic
  **workspace usage cap** (a hard HTTP 400) the LLM half does **not** retry-loop:
  it parks the job (`labels_state=deferred`, no attempt burned), acks so the queue
  drains, and emits `checkpoint_analysis.usage_cap_deferred`. Recover with
  `repo-activity replay-deferred-analysis` once the cap lifts — see
  [`docs/runbooks/checkpoint-analysis-usage-cap.md`](docs/runbooks/checkpoint-analysis-usage-cap.md).
  Health probes only.
- **api** (`cmd/api`) — the unified HTTP server. It serves the activity surface
  **in-process** over both stores — the caller's `/me/*` reads (commits,
  checkpoints, activity, recap) from the user store, plus the repo / contributor
  **aggregates** from the repo store — and, via the absorbed gateway
  (`internal/gateway`), merges that surface with the cell's other services'
  OpenAPI specs (entiredb's git plane) into one document and reverse-proxies
  their requests, following entiredb's replica redirects server-side. No NATS, no
  workers. Replaces the GitHub-webhook-fed activity APIs in `entire.io/api`
  (`cache.ts`, `me.ts`, `recap.ts`) and the standalone `api-gateway`.

The workers' background consumers — index jobs, checkpoint analysis, lifecycle
projections — are inventoried in [`docs/jobs.md`](docs/jobs.md): each job kind and
consumer, the stream that feeds it, the worker that binds it, and its enable gate.

The product surface is primary: it owns the bare `/api/v1/...` (`/me`, `/repos`,
and the project-scoped Trails under `/{host}/{project}`). entiredb's proxied git
plane is sub-pathed under `/api/v1/git/...`,
so the two merge into one served spec without collision. The product surface is
injected as an in-process upstream (`config.NewLocalUpstream`), so its half of
the API costs no network hop and no spec fetch — there is no `ACTIVITY_SPEC_URL`.

The API returns residency-safe **pointers** (`repo_id`, `jurisdiction`, `sha`,
`checkpoint_id`); the actual content (commit messages, checkpoint prompts,
diffs) is fetched from the **Repo API** (the git server), never served here.

## API

All operations live under `/api/v1` (the paths in the tables below are relative
to it; the OpenAPI document and docs UI stay at `/api/v1`),
authenticated with a bearer JWT from entire-core — the only accepted
credential — in one shape: the **account access token** (`aud` = the issuing
core's own host, no scope requirement). The jurisdiction identity token is no
longer accepted.

The token is verified against the JWKS of the core named in its `iss` — every
regional core listed in `ENTIRE_TRUSTED_ISSUERS` (`issuer=jwksURL,…`), so a
caller whose home region mints its tokens elsewhere authenticates here; an
issuer outside that list is rejected before any signature work. With the list
unset the cell falls back to `CORE_JWKS_URL` alone (its own region only). The
token's audience is that of the issuer it was dispatched to, so each trusted
core admits its own. `home_jurisdiction` rides on the token, so `/me` reads it
directly — no per-request Core `/me` call.

| Method | Path | Returns |
|--------|------|---------|
| GET | `/me` | identity + jurisdictions (drives cross-region federation) |
| GET | `/me/commits` | my commits in `?timeframe`/`?since`/`?until` |
| GET | `/me/checkpoints` | my checkpoints in window + `hasCheckpoints` |
| GET | `/me/activity` | daily buckets + per-repo + per-agent + streak; `?repo_ids=` narrows |
| GET | `/me/recap` | per-agent aggregates + summary; `?repo=` adds team column (federated if foreign) |

The table above is the `/me/*` surface (user store). All of it is served by the
single **api** process, alongside the repo aggregates below. The product
surface's OpenAPI document is merged with the cell's other services into one
served spec (at the gateway root, e.g. `/openapi.yaml`); its operations also
remain available directly under `/api/v1` with docs at `/api/v1/docs`. Health:
`/healthz`, `/readyz` (the workers expose these too, with no API surface).

The api process also serves the repo / contributor **aggregates** (metadata +
pointers only — content via the Repo API). A repository — and the project that
owns it — is hosted in a **single jurisdiction** (a project's repos are
co-located with it), so each aggregate is **complete within that region**.
Authz is fail-closed: the caller must have read access (`403` denied / `503` on
Core error), and a repo not in this region returns `404`.

| Method | Path | Returns |
|--------|------|---------|
| GET | `/repos/{id}/summary` | headline rollup (commits, checkpoints, contributors, tokens, lines, active days) |
| GET | `/repos/{id}/activity` | time buckets, `?granularity=day\|week` (UTC) |
| GET | `/repos/{id}/contributors` | leaderboard by author email, `?sort=commits\|checkpoints\|tokens\|lines` |
| GET | `/repos/{id}/agents` | the saved agents that run in the repository, with their latest run and reading there |
| GET | `/repos/{id}/commits` | commit metadata, keyset-paginated (`?cursor`) |
| GET | `/repos/{id}/checkpoints` | checkpoint metadata, keyset-paginated |
| GET | `/repos/{id}/checkpoints/{cid}` | one checkpoint's metadata + linked commit shas |
| GET | `/trails?projectId={id}` | Trails within exactly one project; filtering, grouping, exact counts, and keyset pagination |
| GET | `/trails/facets?projectId={id}` | requested facets for that project's filtered Trail collection |

List and facet reads require exactly one `projectId`. Missing, empty, repeated,
or comma-separated multiple scopes return `400`; there is no unscoped read.
Address the collection directly on the appropriate API endpoint. The handler
resolves only that project's metadata and checks its scoped permissions without
enumerating project affiliations. Public/repository-scoped browsing does not require project
discovery. `repoId` is an optional filter inside the required project, never an
alternative scope; a repository from another project is rejected.

The existing internal `ProjectDirectory.BatchGet` resolves project metadata by
ID, including for empty projects. No Core API, permission, or
protobuf changes are needed. Collections return `projectId`, not redundant
project-reference metadata. No internal-name parsing or public-shell discovery
is required. Caller-specific management uses the existing authorized project
endpoint by ID; directory metadata never grants content access.

Primary-cell selection and wrong-cell handling are general routing concerns,
outside this collection consolidation. There is no Trail-specific forwarding,
destination URL template, redirect, or cell-discovery fallback. The collection
retains its existing jurisdiction and authorization boundaries; existing
repository-primary checks for Change operations are unchanged.

=== crdb-cluster ===
resource "cockroach_cluster" "this" {
  name           = var.name
  cloud_provider = var.cloud_provider
  plan           = var.plan

  # Serverless config (BASIC/STANDARD). Null for ADVANCED, which carries its
  # capacity in the `dedicated` block instead. BASIC clusters omit usage_limits
  # (no provisioned-capacity concept); STANDARD sets the provisioned vCPU usage
  # limit. upgrade_type applies to both (BASIC only supports AUTOMATIC, which
  # the API enforces).
  serverless = var.plan == "ADVANCED" ? null : {
    upgrade_type = var.upgrade_type
    usage_limits = var.plan == "BASIC" ? null : {
      provisioned_virtual_cpus = var.provisioned_virtual_cpus
    }
  }

  # Dedicated config (ADVANCED only). Null for serverless plans. Required for
  # regions CockroachDB only offers on the Advanced tier (e.g. ap-southeast-2).
  dedicated = var.plan == "ADVANCED" ? {
    num_virtual_cpus = var.dedicated_num_virtual_cpus
    storage_gib      = var.dedicated_storage_gib
    disk_iops        = var.dedicated_disk_iops
  } : null

  regions = [
    for r in var.regions : {
      name = r.name
      # `primary` is a serverless-only attribute — the provider rejects it on
      # ADVANCED (dedicated) clusters, whose multi-region primary is set per
      # database via SQL, not on the cluster. Omit it (null) for ADVANCED.
      primary = var.plan != "ADVANCED" && length(var.regions) > 1 ? coalesce(r.primary, false) : null
      # node_count applies only to dedicated clusters. Null (== omitted) for
      # serverless, so existing STANDARD clusters render unchanged.
      node_count = var.plan == "ADVANCED" ? r.node_count : null
    }
  ]

  delete_protection = var.delete_protection
  backup_config     = var.backup_config
  labels            = var.labels

  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = var.plan != "ADVANCED" || (var.dedicated_num_virtual_cpus != null && var.dedicated_storage_gib != null)
      error_message = "ADVANCED clusters require dedicated_num_virtual_cpus and dedicated_storage_gib."
    }
    precondition {
      condition     = var.plan != "ADVANCED" || alltrue([for r in var.regions : coalesce(r.node_count, 0) > 0])
      error_message = "ADVANCED clusters require node_count > 0 on every region."
    }
    # This is what actually surfaces a stray `primary` on an ADVANCED cluster:
    # the regions block above renders primary = null for ADVANCED, so without
    # this check a mistaken `primary = true` would be silently dropped rather
    # than rejected.
    precondition {
      condition     = var.plan != "ADVANCED" || alltrue([for r in var.regions : !coalesce(r.primary, false)])
      error_message = "ADVANCED (dedicated) clusters do not support a primary region; omit `primary` on all regions and set the database primary region via SQL instead."
    }
    precondition {
      condition     = var.plan == "ADVANCED" || length(var.regions) == 1 || length([for r in var.regions : r if coalesce(r.primary, false)]) == 1
      error_message = "Serverless (BASIC/STANDARD) multi-region clusters must mark exactly one region as primary."
    }
  }
}

# IP allowlist entries. Each CIDR is permitted to reach the cluster's public SQL
# and/or DB Console endpoint. Supported on every plan — BASIC, STANDARD, and
# ADVANCED all honour allowlists (CockroachDB Cloud caps entries at 50 for
# serverless, 20 for Advanced on AWS). Empty here creates no resources.
#
# IMPORTANT for serverless (BASIC/STANDARD): a freshly created cluster ships with
# a default "0.0.0.0/0 — allow all" entry that this module does NOT manage.
# Adding entries here does not remove it, so the cluster stays open to the world
# until that default is deleted out-of-band (Cloud console or `ccloud cluster
# networking allowlist delete`). Add the entries below first, confirm callers
# still connect, then remove 0.0.0.0/0.
resource "cockroach_allow_list" "this" {
  for_each = { for e in var.allow_list : e.name => e }

# Global-DB region locality: this cell's CRDB gateway region is not a region of
# the global `entirecore` database (entiredb #2922).
#
# entire-core probes the GLOBAL pool once at startup and every 15 minutes with
#   SELECT gateway_region(), gateway_region() = default_to_database_primary_region(gateway_region())
# and reports the result as the gauge entirecore.globaldb.gateway_region_local
# (1 local / 0 mismatch), tagged gateway_region (CRDB style, e.g.
# aws-ap-south-1). Both modes emit it: global mode's single pool IS the global
# DB, regional mode holds a global pool beside its cell pool.
#
# 0 means the region is in the global CRDB *cluster* but was never added to the
# *database*, and the crdb_region DEFAULT — default_to_database_primary_region(
# gateway_region()) — swallows that silently: REGIONAL BY ROW rows written from
# this cell home in the PRIMARY region instead of locally, so every read and
# write of them pays a cross-region hop while the pods look perfectly healthy.
# It bit us in prod in Jul 2026 (aws-ap-south-1 in the cluster, not in the
# database, Mumbai rows homed in Ohio) and nothing was watching. Operator fix is
# one online statement — see the message below.
#
# Multi-alert by gateway_region so one bad cell pages once, with its region
# named in the notification (that name is the argument to the ALTER). No `by
# {env}`: this module is instantiated per cluster, so the query is already
# scoped to a single (cluster, env) via kube_cluster_name and var.environment is
# baked into the name/message and the env: monitor tag.
locals {
  # Companion board for the gauge (entiredb #2922). Hand-created in Datadog, not
  # managed by this module — the monitor's dashboard_url tag still points at the
  # canonical entire-core board via local.dashboard_line.
  globaldb_region_dashboard_url = "https://app.datadoghq.com/dashboard/kuz-h4d-8f9"

  globaldb_region_runbook_url = "${local.runbook_base}/new-region-standup.md"

  # Verbose operator writeup (prod / verbose_messages = true) vs. a terse
  # one-liner (nonprod). Both keep the ${local.notify_target} routing handle.
  globaldb_region_local_message_verbose = <<-EOT
    The global `entirecore` database has no region for gateway region `{{gateway_region.name}}` — reported by entire-core on ${var.cluster_name} (${var.environment}).

    Every REGIONAL BY ROW row this cell writes is homing in the database's PRIMARY region, not locally: the crdb_region DEFAULT `default_to_database_primary_region(gateway_region())` returns the primary region instead of erroring when the gateway region is unknown to the database. The data is correct and nothing is failing — it is just permanently remote, so every read and write of those rows pays a cross-region hop.

    Fix (online, against the **global-v2** admin DSN — not the regional cluster, and not the CRDB Cloud console SQL shell, which cancels statements over ~10s):

    ```
    ALTER DATABASE entirecore ADD REGION "{{gateway_region.name}}";
    SHOW REGIONS FROM DATABASE entirecore;
    ```

    `entirecore` runs SURVIVE ZONE FAILURE, so ADD REGION is unconstrained (no 3-region minimum) — but do not run it while a locality-changing migration is mid-flight. `spicedb` on the same cluster needs the region too — for replica placement, not row homing — and this monitor does not cover it. Check it while you are here: `SHOW REGIONS FROM DATABASE spicedb`.

    Runbook: ${local.globaldb_region_runbook_url}#4b-app-secrets-after-the-step-8-crdb-apply-before-fleet-reconciles (step 1b, added in https://github.com/entirehq/infra/pull/975)
    Region-locality board: ${local.globaldb_region_dashboard_url}${local.dashboard_line}

    ${local.notify_target}
  EOT

  globaldb_region_local_message_terse = <<-EOT
    The global `entirecore` database has no region for gateway region `{{gateway_region.name}}` (${var.cluster_name}, ${var.environment}) — this cell's REGIONAL BY ROW writes are homing in the primary region, not locally.

    Fix against the global-v2 admin DSN: `ALTER DATABASE entirecore ADD REGION "{{gateway_region.name}}";`

    Runbook: ${local.globaldb_region_runbook_url} (step 1b)

1121 entire-api/docs/architecture.md
# entire-api — architecture

`entire-api` serves **residency-safe activity reads** for Entire: a user's own
commits / checkpoints / recap (`/me/*`), and the repo / contributor / project
aggregates, checkpoint/session lists, and transcripts that power team
dashboards. It is the successor to the GitHub-webhook-fed activity endpoints in
`entire.io/api` (`cache.ts`, `me.ts`, `recap.ts`).

Git data (commit lists, diffs, branch reachability, raw transcripts) is **not
replicated locally** — it is read **through to entiredb** (the regional git
server) at request time and cached keyed by the branch tip, so a ref move
invalidates naturally. The local stores hold only the product overlay
(checkpoints, sessions, their commit links) plus a default-branch commit-metrics
rollup that backs the team aggregates.

Two facts shape every part of the design:

1. **Data has a residence.** A repo's full history (messages, prompts, diffs)
   lives only in the repo's own jurisdiction. A person's cross-repo activity
   must be readable from *their* home region even when the repos live elsewhere
   — but only as **residency-safe metadata** (counts, IDs, timestamps), never
   content.
2. **The API never serves content.** Responses are **pointers** (`repo_id`,
   `jurisdiction`, `sha`, `checkpoint_id`) plus aggregates. The actual content
   is fetched separately from the regional **Repo API** (the git server).

This document is the deep reference. For the surface-level tour and the API
tables, see [`../README.md`](../README.md); for the domain vocabulary
(authn/authz, access gate, fail-closed) see [`../CONTEXT.md`](../CONTEXT.md).

> Diagrams are hand-authored SVGs in [`diagrams/`](diagrams/); regenerate them
> with `python3 docs/diagrams/gen.py`.

---

## 1. System context

![System context: regional activity services vs. the central entire-core control plane](diagrams/01-context.svg)

`entire-core` is the **central control plane**: it publishes the JWKS the
caller's identity token is verified against, resolves identities on its internal
mTLS listener (an account ULID to home placement, `GET /accounts/{id}`, and a
commit author's email to its Entire account, `lookupAuthorAccounts`), serves
repo metadata (`GetRepo`), and owns the runner admission decision every launch
asks for (`POST /runner-admission`, §8). The ingester reads the Repo API with
its own workload cert (cert-only; §8), not a Core-issued token. Read-time
authorization is **not** a Core call — it queries the regional read-only
SpiceDB (§6). Everything else — the three activity processes,
two Postgres stores, the NATS island, and the Repo API — is **regional**,
deployed once per jurisdiction.

---

## 2. Processes

`activity` is **one Go module compiled into several deployable binaries**. They
share `internal/server` for lifecycle (OTel + HTTP + graceful shutdown via an
`errgroup`) but have disjoint responsibilities.

| Binary | Package | Role | Owns | NATS? | API surface |
|--------|---------|------|------|-------|-------------|
| **repo-activity** | `cmd/repo-activity` | Ref consumer + index-jobs consumers + forwarder **publisher** | repo store | yes (consumes `repo_refs_v1` + `repo_index_jobs_v2`, publishes `user_activity_v1`) | health only |
| **user-activity** | `cmd/user-activity` | Forwarder **consumer** | user store | yes (consumes `user_activity_v1`) | health only |
| **activity-api** | `cmd/activity-api` | HTTP read API | reads both stores | **no** | full `/api/v1/*` |
| **runner** | `cmd/runner` | Runner-machine worker: provisions sandboxes, prompts the agent, polls output (see `docs/jobs.md`) | reads and writes repo store run state | yes (three `runner_work_v1` durables) | health only |

Subcommands (cobra): every binary has `serve` + `version`; the workers add
`migrate` (each owns its store's migrations); `repo-activity` adds `backfill`.

The workers bind NATS consumers (index jobs, checkpoint analysis, lifecycle
projections); the api process binds none, though it dials NATS to publish
runner work when `RUNNER_LAUNCH_ENABLED` is set. [`jobs.md`](jobs.md) inventories every
one — its stream, its binary, and its enable gate.

![The three processes (repo-activity, user-activity, activity-api) and the two stores](diagrams/02-processes.svg)

Splitting the API into its own process (commit `dd2bd32`) means the read path
scales and deploys independently of ingest. Its NATS use is limited to
publishing runner work and, with `REF_EVENTS_STREAM_ENABLED`, the ref-events
stream.

---

## 3. Data stores

One PostgreSQL database per region (`internal/store`), split into two schemas:
`repo` and `usr`. No query joins the two halves, and the API keeps a
separate pool per store. Postgres roles enforce that boundary: per-store
read/write and read-only roles are each granted only their own schema, and
every process assumes the role for its use case through its connection string.
The workers write their own store (`repo_rw` / `user_rw`); the `api` process is
read-only on the repo store (`repo_ro`) but read-write on the user store
(`user_rw`), because the user store holds API-native tables (`user_preferences`)
written on a request, not forwarded in. The boundary is **soft** (the login can
`RESET ROLE`); it exists to stop accidental cross-store queries, not a determined
caller. See [ADR 0001](adr/0001-store-boundary-via-roles.md). Migrations track versions in
**distinct goose tables** (`goose_activity_repo` / `goose_activity_user`) so the
two histories never collide.

### 3.1 Repo store (`REPO_DATABASE_DSN`)

The **product overlay** for repos that **live in this region**: checkpoints,
materialised sessions, the checkpoint↔commit links, and a default-branch
commit-metrics rollup. It is **not** a git replica — commit lists, diffs, branch
reachability and raw transcripts are read **through to entiredb** at request
time (see *Read-through to entiredb* below). It is the source of truth for the
checkpoint/session product data and for the residency-safe metadata that gets
forwarded out.

> **Project / repo co-location.** A project is hosted in a single region, and
> every repo it owns lives in that same region (a repo's region *is* its owning
> project's region). So this store holds every repo of any project hosted here,
> so an aggregate computed over a project's repos would be **complete** — never
> a partial cross-region slice. (entire-api serves no project-scoped aggregate
> today; the co-location property is what makes the repo store's view of any
> hosted project whole.)

![Store schema (repo + usr): repos, checkpoints, checkpoint_commits, sessions, repo_checkpoint_analyses, session_shares, repo_branch_tip, repo_author_day, github_repo_meta, repo_runner_settings, sync_state, plus the usr-schema my_activity / user_preferences / user_repo_preferences](diagrams/03-repo-store-er.svg)

_The diagram spans both schemas; the three `usr` tables below the dashed divider are detailed in [§3.2](#32-user-store-user_database_dsn)._

The tables:

- **`repos`** — minimal repo metadata (owning project, jurisdiction).
- **`trails`** — project-scoped intent, metadata, and lifecycle. A Trail has an
  immutable ULID plus a project-local number; `trail_repositories` records its
  explicit repository visibility scope. Scope rows are historical references,
  not authorization facts: every read re-joins `repos` and requires its current
  `owning_project_id` to match the Trail, so a repository transfer cannot expose
  the old project's intent. Transferred Changes retain their parent and scope
  until attachment in the repository's new project atomically replaces the stale
  owner. Scope cleanup refuses to orphan work; reparent first, then remove scope.
- **`repo_trails.trail_id`** — the required project Trail parent for repository/branch
  code work. Multiple Changes may share a parent. The
  empty `trail_changes` table remains temporarily for old binaries' queries during
  rolling deployment; new code neither reads nor writes it. `trail_attached_at` and
  `trail_attached_by` record attachment order and attribution without changing
  the backing work's ID, number, timestamps, or history. Parent scope remains a
  deferred composite FK; parent deletion is restricted rather than cascading
  or silently orphaning code work. A delete trigger preserves the former mapping
  FK's protection against raw deletion of owned backing rows.
  The legacy repository delete path rejects current-project Changes. The
  deprecated project Change DELETE authenticates and checks access, then returns
  `409` without write locks, ETag mutation, or removal events. Atomic reparenting
  records `change_removed` on the former parent; scope cleanup never releases
  ownership.
- **`trail_lifecycle_events`** — the append-only create/update/status and Change
  ownership history for project-scoped Trails.

Project Trails expose the same `type` (`bug`, `feature`, `task`), `priority`
(`urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low`, `none`), and assignee semantics as the
repository Trail UI. Defaults are `task`, `none`, and `assignees: []`. An
assignee is an actor reference — `ulid:<account id>` or `@username` (a bare
string is a username, resolved through Core) — and only the account id is
stored; an unknown username is a 422 (ENT-2922). `assigneeAccountIds` is
position-aligned with `assignees`. Assigning someone never grants access. These are first-class fields,
independent of the caller-defined `metadata` object. PATCH omission preserves
them; `assignees: []` clears the assignment list. Metadata writes use the same
Trail lock, ETag precondition, and lifecycle transaction as title/status writes.

Project Trails are additive. Their HTTP surface is
`GET/POST /{host}/{project}/trails`, `GET/PATCH /{host}/{project}/trails/{trailId}`,
`POST /{host}/{project}/trails/{trailId}/changes`, and
`GET/PUT/DELETE /{host}/{project}/trails/{trailId}/changes/{changeId}`. The
host and project segments form Core's canonical, case-insensitive public
project reference; `trailId` is strictly the Trail ULID, while `changeId` is the
stable backing Change ULID. The public project segment is not a project's
storage name: GitHub mirror projects use an opaque `gh:mirrors:*` storage key.
Repository and branch are representation fields, never route keys, so branch
slashes and renames do not change Change identity. Repository may be empty while
its display metadata is unresolved; that does not prevent ownership attachment.
Collection requests resolve
project name to ID through the caller-authorized Core API. Addressed requests
first resolve the globally unique Trail ID locally, then validate its project
name through Core's workload-gated ProjectDirectory, preserving repo-only reads
without granting project-wide access.

#### Repository work → project Trail discovery

Repository Trail list/detail reads (both `/repos/{repo_id}/trails/...` and
`/trails/gh/{owner}/{repo}/...`), `/me/trails`, and project Change detail include
an optional `parent` navigation object:

```json
{
  "parent": {
    "id": "01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV",
    "number": 42,
    "projectId": "01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAW",
    "host": "gh",
    "project": "widgets",
    "path": "/api/v1/gh/widgets/trails/01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV",
    "jurisdiction": "eu",
    "primaryProcessingCell": "aws-eu-central-1"
  }
}
```

The outer ID/number still identify repository work; the parent's number is
project-local. Branch renames/releases do not change the link. Write responses
omit this read projection; clients should re-read rather than treat omission
from a write response as a detach.

Discovery is a bounded batch over the returned work IDs. It joins current
repository ownership and the parent's explicit repository scope, then requires
repo Pull, Trails enablement, and processing-primary availability. A repo-only
reader can discover intent through that repo without project View, exactly as
on parent detail; no other repository IDs, title, body, or permissions are
exposed. Transferred work, denied/missing projects, and unresolved public names all
omit `parent`. The stored `repo_trails.trail_id` is mandatory; the authorized
navigation projection remains optional. Linking still uses the server's
ownership checks.

Core remains the naming/routing authority. Native public names come from its
workload-gated ProjectDirectory. A GitHub repository owner is only a candidate:
Core's caller-authorized `GET /projects/resolve/gh/{owner}` must resolve it to
the *same project ID* before a link is returned. Stale/reused namespaces cannot
redirect a link to another project's intent, and `gh:mirrors:*` storage names
never become public paths. Project/reference lookups are cached within each
response, including misses. Core/authorization outages are errors, not an
apparently parentless success.

`path` is relative to the **project's** cell, not necessarily the repo's cell.
The directory's `jurisdiction` and `primaryProcessingCell` are preserved for
client cell/cluster discovery and token selection; they are not inferred from
the repo placement or the caller's home. Missing assignments remain empty—do
not synthesize an API hostname or fall back to the current cell. This is
navigation metadata, not cross-cell forwarding or aggregation. Before a parent
exists, clients can use Core's canonical `/projects/resolve/{host}/{project}`
resolver for explicit project targeting; no Trail needs to be created for
project discovery.

Project intent also owns general discussions, including when its repository
scope and Changes are empty. The backend exposes discussion routes:
`GET/POST /{host}/{project}/trails/{trailId}/discussions`, `GET/PATCH .../discussions/{discussionId}`,
`POST .../discussions/{discussionId}/messages`, `PATCH/DELETE .../messages/{messageId}`, and
`GET .../discussions/stream` (JSON events or SSE with `after` / `Last-Event-ID`). Reads
use the parent's project-view or relevant-repo-pull authorization; writes use the
parent's human edit policy: Core's live `canManageTrails`, local project
write/manage, or push on any repository in the parent's current stored scope
(see [§6](#6-read-api--authorization)). Message editing/deletion stays author-only;
automation-only `write_trails` does not confer discussion access. Every child operation checks containment
under the addressed parent. These routes follow the parent project's region,
never a selected repository's region or processing placement.

The shared thread store uses separate `trail_discussions`, messages, events,
and event-sequence tables, with ownership rooted directly in `trails.id`. There
is no repository anchor or project code-review path. Conversation writes lock the
parent and recheck repository-authorized writers' scope, ownership, and Trails
opt-in before mutating (409 on concurrent changes). They do not update its
metadata ETag, repository counters, or automation outbox. Responses use `discussion`; event envelopes use `discussionId`, and updates
emit `discussion_updated` with a `discussion` projection. Message events remain
`message` / `message_deleted`. Payloads identify project scope with `projectId`
and `trailId` instead of `repo`; `trailNumber` is the parent
number. Projection cursors are sampled before reads and the first page's cursor
is carried through continuation tokens, so resuming may replay, but cannot skip,
concurrent updates. SSE connections periodically reauthorize against
the parent. Existing repository discussions, imports, reviews, and APIs remain
independent; no existing discussion data is moved.

# A generic fan-out engine: extracting the consume → resolve → publish-to-regions runtime

Status: **draft** — uncommitted working doc, not a ratified plan. Verified
against `mirror-pipeline`, `entire-api`, `entiredb`, and `fleet` as of
2026-06-30.

## Why

The "island fan-out" pattern — *pull-subscribe a stream, resolve a routing
decision against entire-core, then publish derived messages into one or more
**regional** NATS islands* — has been re-implemented at least **five** times,
and counting: `cmd/core-fanout` landed mid-design (COR-757) as the newest
hand-rolled copy. Every copy reinvents the same NATS-consumer plumbing; the only
genuinely different code is a thin decode → resolve → publish core.

The smell is concrete, not aesthetic. The ~150-line
subscribe/backoff/ack-nak-term/panic-recovery block is copy-pasted **8+ times**
across the repos, the cross-region publisher exists in two near-identical
forms, and `pkg/otelnats` had already been **lifted verbatim** from
`mirror-pipeline` into `entire-api` (the NATS dial has since been consolidated
out of `mirror-pipeline` into the shared `go-nuts` module — COR-925). Each new fan-out (recent
examples: COR-597 concurrency, COR-615/658 backfills, COR-717 auto-seed) widens
the blast radius of any fix to that plumbing, because the fix has to be made N
times by hand.

The team has, in fact, **already started this extraction**: `internal/natsregions`
was deliberately pulled out of `cmd/fanout` and `cmd/meta-fanout`, and its
package doc already names the abstraction —

> *"The only thing that differs between them is the publisher type and the
> per-placement payload — everything about discovering, dialing, routing to,
> and health-checking the per-cluster NATS connections is identical, so it
> lives here once."*

This doc proposes finishing that job: promote the duplicated **consumer
runtime** and **multi-region transport** into a shared, versioned library so a
developer who needs to "read a stream and fan out" writes three small functions
and a config struct, not a fifth copy of the plumbing.

## Inventory: where the pattern lives today

| Where | Role | What it does | Consumer API | Routing backend |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mirror-pipeline/cmd/fanout` | producer | GitHub `push` → git-sync jobs. US-only. 1 consumer + worker-pool + DLQ. | legacy `PullSubscribe`/`Fetch` | entire-core `RepoLookup` (Connect/gRPC, mTLS) |
| `mirror-pipeline/cmd/meta-fanout` | producer | star/fork/PR meta + verbatim lifecycle pipe + 2 backfills. **4 consumers, 3 archetypes.** Serial, no DLQ. | legacy `PullSubscribe`/`Fetch` | same `RepoLookup` |
| `mirror-pipeline/cmd/core-fanout` *(new, COR-757)* | producer | push → deduped commit-author jobs (`github_push_author`) per placement, so each regional core resolves verified emails locally. `consumer.go` says *"mirroring cmd/meta-fanout."* Serial, no DLQ. | legacy `PullSubscribe`/`Fetch` | same `RepoLookup` |
| `entire-api/internal/forwarder` (+ `reattribute`, `ingest`) | producer | user-activity → publish to recipient's **home-jurisdiction** region. Its own code says it is *"mirroring cmd/fanout"*; `natsdial`/`otelnats` copied verbatim. | **modern `jetstream.Consume`** | `coreapi` (plain HTTP/JSON, mTLS) |
| `entiredb/{permswebhook, verifiedemailwebhook, mirrordone}` | consumer | drain a stream → apply to regional/global store. ~150-line scaffold copy-pasted 3×. | legacy `PullSubscribe`/`Fetch` | implicit (per-jurisdiction durable + home skip) |
| `mirror-pipeline` **repo_refs replicator** *(planned)* | producer | EntireDB post-receive (`repo_refs_v1`, **per-region**) → replica git-sync jobs. Loop-prevented (skip `local_region != home_region`). Same `mirror_git_v1` output as `cmd/fanout`. | modern `jetstream.Consume` | core replica-lookup (returns `replicas[]` + `source_url`) |

Two facts shape everything below:

1. **The actual cross-region fan-out *hop* exists in two repos** (mirror-pipeline
   and entire-api). entiredb's permission / verified-email flows are the
   **consumer side**. The old `cmd/fanout → mirror_perms_v1 → permsconsumer`
   republish hop was **deleted (COR-523)** — entire-core now consumes
   `webhooks_github_v1` directly, and cross-region signalling rides
   `resource_lifecycle_v1` via `resourceevents`. (The "verified email from
   core" flow is `verifiedemailwebhook` emitting
   `resource_lifecycle_v1.verified_email.created`, which `entire-api`'s
   `reattribute` then fans out.)
2. **There is no NATS supercluster.** Every region is an independent NATS
   island; cross-region is always an app-level publish from a process holding
   one connection per region. No JetStream `sources`/`mirror` replication exists
   in fleet. A generic library can safely bake this invariant in.

## The abstraction

A fan-out is three steps, and only the middle one is ever unique:

```
generic runtime
  subscribe(stream, durable, filter-subjects) → backoff-retry resubscribe
  per message:
    Decode(subject, bytes) → Event      ◄ PLUGIN    err   → Term
    Filter(Event) → bool  [optional]    ◄ PLUGIN    false → Ack (no-op)
    Resolve(ctx, Event) → []Route       ◄ PLUGIN    err   → Nak
    publish each Route                    engine     Route renders its own
                                                     subject / msg-id / bytes
  Ack / Nak(+delay) / Term · panic → Nak · metrics · /readyz

generic transport  (today: internal/natsregions)
  dial N regions (RetryOnFailedConnect) · route by cluster_id / jurisdiction
  Nats-Msg-Id dedup · local-only readiness gate · region_connected gauge
```

### What the library provides (free)

Everything currently copy-pasted:

- **Consumer runtime** — the subscribe + exponential-backoff resubscribe loop,
  the retry envelope (`AckWait`, `MaxDeliver`, flat `NakWithDelay`), the
  Ack/Nak/Term decision tree, panic→Nak recovery (so one poison-pill delivery
  can't crash-loop every replica), `numDelivered`/`isFinalDelivery`, and
  `/readyz` that gates on the live subscription + local NATS only.
- **Multi-region transport** — `internal/natsregions` is *already* this, and its
  `Resolve[P any]` is *already* generic over publisher type (instantiated today
  with `mirrorjobs.MirrorPublisher`, `*metajobs.Publisher`, `*prjobs.Publisher`).
  Lift it as-is; the only wart is the literal `FANOUT_NATS_REGIONS` env name.
- **Uniform publish** — the three publishers (`gitjobs` / `metajobs` / `prjobs`)
  share an identical body (subject → marshal → `Nats-Msg-Id` → `PublishMsg` with
  a bounded `publishAckWait`), differing *only* in subject / msg-id / payload.
  The engine's transport publishes once and each **`Route` renders itself**, so
  there is no per-job publisher to write — and one consumer can emit several job
  types. *(The prototype confirmed a separate `Publisher[R]` couldn't express
  that; the self-describing Route can — see Prototype validation.)*
- **Metric set** — a name-prefixed common core (`*.completed{event,outcome,
  reason}`, `*.handler_panic`, `*.nats.region_connected`) plus opt-in
  per-feature instruments (worker-pool, extra-consumer outcomes).
- **OTel propagation** — `pkg/otelnats` (Inject/Extract) and `pkg/otelsetup`
  are already domain-free; lift directly.

### What the developer writes (the plugin surface)

```go
// A handler is a Spec, generic only over the decoded event E. Routes are the
// self-describing Route interface (below), so one Resolve can return a
// heterogeneous set — e.g. both github_meta and github_pr jobs from one webhook.
type Spec[E any] struct {
    Decode  func(subject string, data []byte) (E, error)  // required; err/*InputError → Term
    Filter  func(E) bool                                  // optional; false → Ack no-op (loop prevention)
    Resolve func(context.Context, E) ([]Route, error)     // required; err → Nak (*InputError → Term)
    // + Source (stream / durable / filter-subjects / concurrency), Retry, optional DLQ
}

// Route is SELF-DESCRIBING: it renders its own subject, dedup id, and bytes, so
// the engine publishes any route generically and one consumer can fan out
// multiple job types. (This replaced an earlier separate Publisher[R], which the
// prototype showed could not express multi-output — see Prototype validation.)
type Route interface {
    Region() string           // cluster_id or jurisdiction; engine picks the NATS island
    Subject() string
    MsgID() string            // Nats-Msg-Id for idempotent publish
    Marshal() ([]byte, error)
}
```

The `Spec.Source` carries the stream, durable (or a naming strategy), filter
subjects, and concurrency; `Retry` and `DLQ` are opt-in. The engine wires these
into the runtime above.

### The runtime must support N consumers and ≥3 archetypes

`cmd/meta-fanout` already runs **four** consumers in one process and exercises
three structurally-distinct archetypes. The library must model all of them, or
it doesn't actually replace what exists:

| Archetype | Example | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **a. Live envelope-dispatch** | `fanout` push, `meta-fanout` webhook | decode → resolve placements → fan one job per placement |

# Fanout engine — Layer 1: self-describing Routes

Status: proposed · Author: Andrea Nodari · Follows: `fanout-engine-design.md` (Layer 0)

## Where we are

Layer 0 — the consumer runtime (`pkg/fanoutengine`: subscribe/backoff, Ack/Nak/Term
decision tree, panic recovery, flat-NakWithDelay retry envelope, OTel span +
trace propagation, `/readyz`, bounded worker pool, opt-in DLQ) — is **done and
adopted in all three fan-out binaries** (core-fanout #184, meta-fanout #185,
fanout #186).

Layer 1 — multi-region transport + **self-describing Route** — is **half done**:

- ✅ The transport is shared. `internal/natsregions` owns region config parsing,
  remote dial, per-cluster connection health, and the `Resolve[P]` routing rule
  (single-region → local; multi-region → by `cluster_id`, error on an unmapped
  one so the consumer Naks rather than silently going local).
- ❌ The **self-describing Route** — where the engine owns the publish so a binary
  doesn't need its own router — is **not in production**. It was validated in the
  spike (`../fanout/engine/route.go`, `regions.go`, handlers `gitsync`/`meta`/
  `reporefs`) and is the missing rung.

## What's still duplicated (the problem L1 finishes)

Each binary still hand-rolls a thin **router** that does the same
`natsregions.Resolve(...) → publish typed job` dance:

| Binary | Router | Publishes |
|---|---|---|
| fanout | `mirrorPublisherRouter` | `mirrorjobs` sync_repo jobs |
| meta-fanout | `metaPublisherRouter` + `prPublisherRouter` | `metajobs` + `prjobs` |
| core-fanout | (its router) | core jobs |

And the **"publish all routes, Nak if any failed"** partial-failure aggregation is
copy-pasted: `cmd/fanout/dispatch.go::push()` and
`cmd/meta-fanout/dispatch.go::publishMetaToRoutes/publishPRToRoutes`. Two copies
of the same loop, which can (and is the kind of thing that does) drift.

Net: adding a new fan-out consumer (e.g. `repo_refs_v1`) means writing *another*
router + *another* partial-failure loop. That's exactly what L1 removes.

## The design

Lift the spike's self-describing `Route` into `pkg/fanoutengine` (on the **legacy
`nats.JetStreamContext` API**, to stay behavior-preserving — the Route concept is
API-agnostic; only the publish call differs from the spike's modern
`jetstream.JetStream`). The engine gains ownership of resolve→publish→partial-failure;
the binaries shrink to "decode the event, return the routes."

### 1. `Route` — self-describing destination (delegate-publish)

```go
// Route is one resolved destination: one message into one region's island.
// Self-describing so a single Resolve can return a HETEROGENEOUS set (the
// load-bearing case: meta-fanout emits BOTH a metajob and a prjob from one
// webhook — a single typed Publisher[R] can't express that).
type Route interface {
    Region() string                                  // cluster_id / jurisdiction → which island
    Publish(ctx context.Context, js PublishJS) error // render + publish into THIS region's handle
}

// PublishJS is the per-region publish surface (a JetStream context, narrowed to
// the one method the typed publishers use, so tests fake it trivially).
type PublishJS interface {
    PublishMsg(m *nats.Msg, opts ...nats.PubOpt) (*nats.PubAck, error)
}
```

**Why `Publish(ctx, js)` and not the spike's `Subject()/MsgID()/Marshal()`.** The
spike rendered the route to bytes and let the engine do a generic `js.Publish`.
That is fine for a greenfield spike but would **regress observability** here: the
production typed publishers (`mirrorjobs`/`metajobs`/`prjobs`) each emit a
**producer span** (e.g. `mirror.git.publish`), **`otelnats.Inject`** the W3C trace
context into the outgoing message (so the downstream consumer's trace links to
this one), set ack `sequence`/`duplicate` span attrs, and write a structured
publish log. A generic engine publish would drop all of that, and the producer
span *name* differs per publisher — the engine can't reproduce three names
generically. So the Route **delegates the whole publish** to the domain: its
`Publish` simply *is* the existing typed publisher over the engine-resolved
region handle, e.g.

```go
type gitSyncRoute struct{ route mirrorjobs.MirrorRoute }
func (r gitSyncRoute) Region() string { return r.route.Placement.ClusterID }
func (r gitSyncRoute) Publish(ctx context.Context, js fanoutengine.PublishJS) error {
    return mirrorjobs.NewPublisher(js).PublishGitSyncJob(ctx, r.route) // unchanged publish
}
```

Region-resolution and partial-failure move to the engine; the publish itself
(subject, Nats-Msg-Id, marshal, producer span, trace injection, log) stays
verbatim in the domain. A future L2 service can revisit a marshal-based route if
it wants fully generic publish; behavior-preservation here does not.

### 2. `Resolver` — the new plugin contract (replaces `Dispatcher`)

```go
// Resolver turns one decoded envelope into zero or more routes. Empty slice =
// benign no-op (Ack, nothing to fan out — e.g. a webhook for a repo with no
// mirror placement). An *InputError Terminates; any other error Naks. ackReason
// is a benign disposition label recorded on the ack metric (both a publish and
// an empty-routes no-op); consumers that don't distinguish reasons return "".
type Resolver interface {
    Resolve(ctx context.Context, event, deliveryID string, observedAt time.Time, body []byte) (routes []Route, ackReason string, err error)
}
```

### 3. Engine owns region resolution + partial-failure

A `Regions` helper in the engine: `Local PublishJS` + `ByKey map[string]PublishJS`,
applying the same routing rule as `natsregions.Resolve` (single-region → `Local`;
multi-region → by region key, error on an unmapped key → Nak so the operator
fixes the map without losing the message). For each resolved route the engine
looks up the region handle and calls `route.Publish(ctx, js)`. The per-message
flow becomes:

```
decode (Decoder)            → bad envelope → Term + DLQ(bad_envelope)
resolve (Resolver)          → InputError   → Term + DLQ(input_error)
                            → other error  → Nak (Term + DLQ(max_deliveries) on final delivery)
                            → empty routes → Ack (benign no-op)
publish each route (Regions) → all ok      → Ack
                            → any failed   → Nak (Term + DLQ(max_deliveries) on final delivery)
```

This moves the partial-failure aggregation **out of** `push()` /
`publishMetaToRoutes` **into the engine, once**.

## Behavior-preservation contract (the bar)

Same as the L0 conversions — proven by the existing per-binary test suites
passing unchanged. Because the Route **delegates the whole publish** to the
existing typed publisher (§1), the publish itself is preserved *by construction* —
it is the same code path:

- **Subject, Nats-Msg-Id, payload, producer span, `otelnats.Inject` (trace
  propagation), ack-metadata span attrs, and the publish log** are all unchanged:
  `route.Publish` calls `mirrorjobs/metajobs/prjobs.Publisher.Publish*` verbatim.
  This sidesteps what would otherwise be the #1 risk (a drifted Nats-Msg-Id
  silently breaking dedup → double-publish on redelivery).
- **Partial-failure semantics** — publish all routes, Nak if any failed, Term +
  DLQ (`max_deliveries`) on exhaustion. This is the one behavior that *moves*
  (out of `push()` / `publishMetaToRoutes`, into the engine). fanout's current
  semantics become the shared implementation; meta-fanout's variant is reconciled
  to match — intentional, and called out in its PR.
- **Consumer-side DLQ reasons**, **metrics** (outcome/reason/event strings), and
  **consumer spans** (`*.dispatch` name + `entire.*` / `github.*` attrs) —
  unchanged.

# Fanout route memo — duplicate suppression on partial-failure redelivery

Status: accepted (shipped in #200) · Follows: `fanout-engine-l1-design.md`

## Problem

`fanoutengine.dispatchRoutes` publishes ALL routes, then Naks if any region
failed — routes are independent, so one region's outage must not starve the
others. The Nak'd message redelivers ~`NakDelay` (30s) later and fans out
again, **including into the regions that already PubAck'd**.

For `github_meta_v1` / `github_pr_v1` / `github_push_author_v1` that re-publish
is collapsed server-side: their `Nats-Msg-Id` dedup windows (5m) are sized
past the redelivery span. For `mirror_git_v1` it is not: the window is
deliberately **1s**, so every retry re-published a full git-sync job into
every healthy region — a single-region outage multiplying no-op syncs
globally for up to `MaxDeliver`(8) attempts.

## Why the dedup window can't fix it

`mirror_git_v1`'s 1s window is load-bearing in **both** directions (also
documented on the Stream CR in fleet, `apps/nats-streams/base/mirror-git-v1.yaml`):

- The job's msg-id (`op/source/owner/repo/target`) has **no per-push
  component**. A wider window would swallow the sync job for a *follow-up
  push* to the same repo as a "duplicate" — a stale mirror until the next
  push. The window is scoped to collapse only the fan-out burst from a single
  source change (e.g. a multi-ref push arriving as N webhook deliveries).
- The same content-keyed msg-id contract is shared by **entiredb's
  create-time clone publisher** (`core/mirrorrepo/gitjobs`): with a wide
  window, a mirror delete+recreate inside it would lose its initial clone job.
- The rekicker is unaffected either way — it mints a fresh NUID per re-emit
  precisely so re-kicks are never collapsed.

Switching to a delivery-scoped msg-id (the `github_push_author_v1` pattern:
id = webhook delivery id, window ≥ redelivery span) was also rejected: it
gives up the burst-collapse (a 50-tag push becomes 50 sync jobs instead of
~1) and forces the msg-id contract change onto every publisher of the
subject.

## Decision: in-process route memo

The engine keeps a bounded, TTL'd, in-process map (`routememo.go`):

- **record** `(delivery_id, region)` on each successful PubAck;
- **skip** memoized regions when the redelivery lands on the same replica —
  only the failed regions retry (surfaced as
  `entire.dispatch.placements_skipped` on the dispatch span);
- **forget** the entry on every terminal disposition — Ack, input-error Term,
  and *any* final delivery (exhaustion Term, final Nak, final-delivery panic)
  — so a later, separate message reusing the delivery id (a manual GitHub
  redelivery after the ingest stream's dedup window) fans out fresh;
- **TTL** = `MaxDeliver × (AckWait + NakDelay)`, the horizon past which the
  same stream message can no longer redeliver (backstop for the panic path);
- **cap** = 4096 entries (in-limbo deliveries are bounded by MaxAckPending;
  eviction only loses the optimization).

Fail-safety is one-directional by construction: a memo **miss** (other
replica, restart, eviction, TTL) re-publishes everything — exactly the
pre-memo behavior, safe because syncs are idempotent. A false **skip** would
require an entry that was never backed by a PubAck, which the code never
writes.

### What it deliberately does not cover

A redelivery that lands on a **different replica** misses the memo and
re-publishes everywhere. With N fanout replicas, roughly (N−1)/N of retries
hop replicas; because each replica accumulates its own memo, the expected
duplicate fan-out rounds per affected webhook drop from ~`MaxDeliver−1` to
~(distinct replicas hit − 1) — a ~2–3× reduction at N=3, not elimination.

## The durable alternative (considered, deferred)

A NATS KV bucket would close the cross-replica gap. The design we would use
if it becomes justified:

- bucket `KV_fanout_route_memo`, declared in fleet (nack CR, `preventDelete`),
  bucket TTL ≈ the redelivery horizon (~10m), R3 like everything else;
- **read only on redeliveries** (`NumDelivered > 1`) — the first-delivery hot
  path never touches KV;
- **write only on partial failure** (the succeeded-regions set,
  revision-CAS with union-merge for the rare AckWait-expiry race), delete on
  terminal disposition;
- **fail open** on any KV error or slowness: treat as a memo miss and
  publish everything.

fail-open path and CAS-merge discipline to maintain, and a second stateful
system consulted by the dispatch path — all purchased against a residual that
is rare (requires a region partition *and* a replica hop), self-healing, and
idempotent. Note the load argument does **not** hold against it: the KV would
live on the central cluster, which must be healthy for fanout to run at all,
and the redelivery-only read pattern adds nothing to steady state.

// Memory is a projection held in memory.
//
// It exists to be the reference for the deciding-stamp rule and the oracle the
// tests compare against: a SQL projection is a use-case concern, but the rule it
// must implement is not, and stating it once, in one small reference, is better
// than restating it per adapter.
type Memory struct {
	records map[record.Key]*memRecord
}

type memRecord struct {
	fields map[string]held
	floor  stamp.Stamp
}

// held is a value and the class that wrote it.
//
// The class is kept beside the value rather than added to record.Value, which is
// a folded record's own type and is encoded: a field there that nothing writes
// to the wire round-trips as zero, and the next reader of it is wrong.
type held struct {
	class record.Class
	value record.Value
}

// NewMemory returns an empty projection.
func NewMemory() *Memory {
	return &Memory{records: map[record.Key]*memRecord{}}
}

func (m *Memory) at(k record.Key) *memRecord {
	rec, ok := m.records[k]
	if !ok {
		rec = &memRecord{fields: map[string]held{}}
		m.records[k] = rec
	}
	return rec
}

# entire-records

**Structured data for a team, kept in Git instead of a database.**

With entire-records you describe your own record model in a YAML file: types,
how they nest, typed fields, references between them. Apply it, and the repo you
already have becomes a shared, offline-first store, with a full CLI generated
from the schema and sync over plain `git fetch`/`push`. It is a good fit for
planning boards, issue and PR mirrors, review findings, and other team data
that should live next to the code and travel with it. Records are stored on
[strata](https://github.com/entirehq/strata). Every writer appends to its own
log, so many people and agents can write at once without fighting over one
branch, and every push is a fast-forward. Concurrent edits to the same field
resolve per field, and the last writer wins.

Want to see your own schema working? Apply it and run `records-explore`, or run
`./examples/explore.sh` for a seeded throwaway repo. Details are in
[`examples/explorer/`](examples/explorer/README.md).

## Install

```
mise run dev:publish     # installs all four binaries into ~/go/bin
mise run dev:unpublish   # removes them again
```

`entire-records` carries the generic commands. Each `records-*` binary is one
example built on top of it. `go install ./cmd/...` does the same thing.

## Quick start

```
cd your-repo
entire-records init          # points the store's remote at this repo's origin

cat > schema.yaml <<'EOF'
name: roadmap
version: 1

types:
  - name: initiative
    fields:
      - key: name
  - name: project
    parent: initiative
    ordered: true
    fields:
      - key: title
        required: true
      - key: status
        knownValues: [active, done]
      - key: estimate
        type: int
        minimum: 0
        maximum: 21
EOF
entire-records schema apply schema.yaml

entire-records initiative add --name "Q3"
entire-records project add <initiativeId> --title "Ship it"
entire-records project show <projectId>
entire-records sync
```

A fresh repo starts with no types at all; every record command comes from your
schema. Run any command with `--help` for its flags, and `entire-records doctor`
to check that the repo, identity, remote, schemas and records are healthy.

## The examples

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| [`explorer/`](examples/explorer/README.md) | web CRUD for whatever types your schema declares | `records-explore` |
| [`githubsync/`](examples/githubsync/README.md) | incremental mirror of a GitHub repo's issues, PRs and comments | `records-github` |
| [`trailsync/`](examples/trailsync/README.md) | the same for Entire's trails, findings and comments | `records-trails` |

[`entirehq/entire-plans`](https://github.com/entirehq/entire-plans) is a
planning UI built on this repo's published packages.
