input.description: Read strata design doc (middle part)

result.output:
| 100 | 64 KiB | 53ms | 51ms | 1 against 100 |
| 400 | 64 KiB | 64ms | 42ms | 1 against 400 |
| 400 | 256 KiB | 133ms | 40ms | 1 against 400 |

**Reading the newest is flat and folding the partition is not.** The right-hand
column is the structural claim and does not depend on a clock: one record read
where the fold reads four hundred. The timings say when that matters, and the
answer is honest — **below a few MiB in a partition it does not.** Both paths cost
the same two subprocesses, git's fixed ~40ms swamps the difference, and at 4 KiB
the ordered read is marginally *slower*. The gap opens where the payload does: at
400 consolidations of 256 KiB the fold is reading 100 MiB to keep one of them, and is
3× slower with no bound on how much worse it gets.

Which is the case it was built for. A consolidation carries a whole document, nothing
expires consolidations, and the only question ever asked of them is which is newest —
so the fold decoded every version a document ever had to discard all but one.

**Consolidations and not updates, and the reason is roll-up.** A bundle is one blob
holding many records at one id, so nothing a listing can see says whether a range
reaches into one and every bundle is fetched whole. Updates are precisely the type
that rolls up, so ordering them would buy less the longer a document lived. See
[ADR-0016](adr/0016-an-ordered-type-keeps-its-ids-in-its-paths.md), which also
records why a real radix tree is barred: collapsing single-child chains is
deterministic, but it makes a record's path a function of the whole record set
rather than of its own key, and `History` computes one key's path across every
generation.

Roll-up had to change with it. A bundle used to be keyed by the writer whose
records it replaced; now it is keyed by partition *and* writer, because a bundle
spanning a hundred documents would land in whichever partition the writer's own
name hashed to, and no reader of those documents would look there. That is the
third time roll-up has cut across a read path — the first returned an empty
document — so it has a test of its own at each level.

**Undo is a compensating write, and history is what a generation happened to
keep.** `History(type, id, field)` returns the values a mutable field has held,
oldest first. The grain is not uniform and cannot be: a generation records what
was current at its boundary, not how it got there, so several writes between two
boundaries leave one revision once the log holding them is pruned. Above the
newest boundary the tail still has every op, so recent changes are complete. Fine
in the present, coarse in the past — which is the shape an editor wants and is not
an audit log, since a value that existed for a second between two boundaries can
be gone with nothing to say it was there. How far back it reaches is exactly how
many generations retention keeps.

Undoing is then an ordinary write:

    revs, _ := s.History("plan", "p", "title")
    restore, current := revs[len(revs)-2], revs[len(revs)-1]
    s.Begin().SetIf("plan", "p", "title", restore.Value.Bytes, current.Value.Stamp).Commit()

`SetIf` records the stamp the write believed it was overwriting. It is not a
compare-and-swap and nothing here could make it one — this is last-writer-wins
across clones that may not have spoken in a week — but an undo decided against a
value somebody has since replaced is reported as a conflict rather than silently
winning or silently losing. That is the difference worth having: the caller can
show somebody what happened.

The other three classes have no such thing, and say so rather than returning an
empty history that reads as "nothing happened". A mirrored record's history is
upstream's. An immutable fact never changes. A whole record has no single value.

**A shared append-only log would undo the premise.** gittuf is an appealing answer
to the largest gap here — it has the key distribution, rotation and revocation
this project's signing deliberately does not, and it keeps policy in the
repository rather than in a forge, which is the stance taken everywhere else. It
also records every reference update as an entry in one hash-chained log under
`refs/gittuf/reference-state-log`. Every writer appends to that one ref, and each
entry names its predecessor, so concurrent appends cannot merge: a loser must
fetch, rebuild its entry and try again. Reproduce with `mise run gittuf-cost`.

| writers | log appends | own refs refused | elapsed | attempts per append | gave up after 12 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 20 | 0 | 4.3s | 2.5 | 0 |
| 8 | 40 | 0 | 13.4s | 4.5 | 0 |
| 16 | 80 | 0 | 43.1s | 7.4 | 9 |

Eight writers pushing only their own refs, for comparison: **0.41s, nothing
refused**. The retry count grows with the writer count rather than staying flat,
which is what a single serialisation point looks like from the outside, and at
sixteen writers nine appends of eighty never landed at all.

None of that is a criticism of gittuf, which is built for human-paced pushes to a
handful of branches, where one log entry per push costs nothing. It is a
statement about this design's push pattern — one per writer per sync, continuously
— being outside that envelope. The usable combination is gittuf's policy model,
its keys and rotation and thresholds, without a log entry on the per-writer push
path.

**So authorization is a pre-receive hook over a policy on the server's disk.**
Write access to a repository is push access to every store in it, and git has no
per-ref authorization, so the boundary a group gets is whatever the server
enforces at receive time. `cmd/strata-receive` is that hook; `authz` is the
decision it makes, with no git in it. A grant is per writer rather than per store,
generated by `authz.Grant`:

    allow alice refs/strata/alpha/log/W1/*
    allow alice refs/strata/alpha/announced/W1
    allow alice refs/strata/alpha/evicted/W1
    allow alice refs/strata/alpha/gen/*

Generated, because the ref layout is the protocol's business and a hand-written
policy is a second copy of it that diverges quietly. The mistake worth designing
out is one `refs/strata/alpha/*` line: it hands every member every other member's
log, and it looks reasonable.

The fourth line is here because generating it was not enough on its own. `authz`
generated three and named the kinds of ref itself, which is a second copy by
another route: the layout gained an eviction ref, the grant did not, and the hook
had no case for one — so it refused the very push that releases the barrier, and
no test could see it, because seeing it needed the store's half and the hook's
half in view at once. Both halves are now `reflayout`, and an import-boundary test
fails on any shipped code that spells a record ref out for itself.

**Ending a writer needs a different grant, and it is broad on purpose.** `Evict`
and `Retire` act on somebody else's refs, which a per-writer grant cannot express
— so for a while the two operational verbs this ships could not be used against a
deployment running the hook at all, and eviction is what releases a stalled
barrier. `authz.Operator` generates the answer:

    allow-create ops refs/strata/alpha/evicted/*
    allow-delete ops refs/strata/alpha/evicted/*
    allow-delete ops refs/strata/alpha/announced/*
    allow-delete ops refs/strata/alpha/log/*

A policy line carries a direction, and `allow` still means any of them, so a file
written before this means what it always did. The breadth above is affordable only
because the verb that would let an operator *append* to somebody's log is not
there: ending a writer creates an eviction and deletes refs, and never moves one
from one value to another. A deletion is loud — the ref is gone and `strata check`
says what dangles — where a forged append is silent and attributed to whoever did
not write it. See
[ADR-0015](adr/0015-an-operator-grant-withholds-a-verb-rather-than-narrowing-a-pattern.md).

**A writer nobody can name is authorised by its shape.** A one-shot writer's
identity is 130 bits of `crypto/rand` minted as it commits — it has to be, because
two processes claiming one identity would reuse sequence numbers and diverge
silently — so no grant can name it, and CI reporting worked against a server that
authorises nothing and against no other kind. `authz.OneShot` grants the shape:

    allow-oneshot ci refs/strata/alpha

which permits `announced/<W>`, `log/<W>/0` and `evicted/<W>` arriving together,
as creations, for one `W`. That is the glossary's definition of a one-shot
writer turned into a predicate, and the hook can decide it because a
`pre-receive` sees every ref a push proposes at once. It cannot be grafted onto
an existing writer — that writer's announcement is already there, so naming it
is not a creation — it cannot append later, and it cannot introduce a writer
that does not evict itself, which turns
[ADR-0002](adr/0002-a-one-shot-writer-evicts-itself.md)'s contract from a
convention into a condition of being let in. See
[ADR-0018](adr/0018-a-one-shot-writer-is-authorised-by-shape.md).

Two rules hold for everyone, policy or no policy. **A published generation may be
created or deleted, never replaced** — it is verified by recomputation, which
works only while the bytes at a number stay the bytes everyone folded, and a
replacement leaves nothing a later read could notice. And **a ref shape the layout
does not describe is refused**, because under the published ref prefix there is no
third case worth waving through.

The identity comes from the environment, set by the server's access layer, and
never from a push option: those are sent by the client as part of the push being
authorized. A missing policy denies. The tests are hermetic — a real bare
repository, the real hook, real pushes from a real store — and they prove the
hook, not authentication: a path remote has none, since `receive-pack` runs as a
child of the pushing process. See
[ADR-0012](adr/0012-push-authorization-is-a-server-side-policy.md).

**Durability costs about 8ms an append, and we pay it.** git's default is
`core.fsync=committed,-loose-object` — it does not sync a loose object at all —
and on macOS the default `core.fsyncMethod` is `writeout-only`, which git's own
documentation says may not survive a system crash. A log entry is a commit, so
that is our data, and the failure it allows is worse than losing a write: the ref
update can land while the object it names does not, leaving a dangling reference
no read can recover from.

| | median append |
| --- | --- |
| git's defaults | 63.0ms |
| `core.fsync=loose-object,pack,ref`, `fsyncMethod=batch` | 71.3ms |

13%, and most of the 63ms is subprocess spawn rather than git.

Which repositories get those settings is a question about who asked. `store.Open`
attaches to a store and writes nothing: a projector reading one must not be the
thing that reconfigures it, so a repository it was merely pointed at keeps
whatever it had and `strata check` reports it. `store.Prepare` is the other verb —
create the repository if it is not one, wire the remote, make writes crash-safe,
announce this writer — and it does write those two settings, into a repository it
may not have created. That is the point of asking for it, and `strata init` is the
command that does. Worth knowing before pointing it at a repository somebody else
configured.

The distinction used to be a comment in the CLI rather than a rule. Three callers
wrote the sequence out by hand and two left the crash-safety line out of it, so a
store put into an existing repository was crash-safe or not according to which one
had set it up.

**Ops cost about 60 bytes** raw, 76 armoured. Git refuses a NUL byte in a commit
message and silently re-encodes anything above `0x7f` as UTF-8 — both verified
against git, not assumed — so a payload in a message must be pure ASCII. ascii85
costs +25% against base64's +33% and is in the standard library. For contrast,
`records-wal-db` measured 240 bytes/op for JSONL, and base64 CBOR would be around
117 because it cannot intern writer ids.

That armouring is the trade: an uncompacted log is about 18% larger on disk than
the blob layout was, in exchange for a quarter of the objects and no write
amplification. A compacted clone is the same size either way. Compressing the
payload before armouring would recover it, and is safe for logs specifically —
they are written once by one writer and never re-derived, so unlike a generation
they carry no byte-identity requirement.

## Running it

```
mise run check      # format, vet, race, and the property suite at depth
mise run sweep      # concurrency and convergence at higher clone counts
mise run gates      # the measured numbers above
go test ./... -deep 40
```

The race leg runs `-parallel 1`. Driving the git binary means a fork per
operation, and under `-race` each fork copies a ThreadSanitizer-instrumented
address space; enough at once and TSan fails an assertion inside the forked child
rather than reporting anything about this code. The giveaway is that no
`DATA RACE` is printed — what appears is `CHECK failed: tsan_rtl.cpp` on a git
subprocess's stderr. Serialised it is clean, so the detector keeps its coverage
over everything it does find, and the leg costs about five minutes; see
[ADR-0001](adr/0001-we-drive-the-git-binary-not-go-git.md).

Which git drives a store is a caller's choice: `store.Open` takes a `git.Driver`
for objects, refs and configuration and a `git.Transport` for the wire, and the
two are chosen separately. `gitbin` is the binary and is what everything here
runs on; `git/conformance` is the suite any second implementation has to answer,
including object ids pinned as fixtures, because two clones that disagree by a
byte publish rival generations forever. See
[ADR-0020](adr/0020-a-transport-is-chosen-separately-from-a-repository.md).

A driver that cannot offer an atomic multi-ref update can still hold a writer. The
whole of a durable writer's life moves one ref at a time, and every operation
needing several at once is maintenance, so such a store appends, pushes what it
alone owns, and refuses to compact, prune, retain, retire or begin a one-shot
draft. Pushing a generation is the exception that proves the rule: it can end in
adopting a rival, which is a transaction — and a clone that has never compacted
holds no generation ref to offer. See
[ADR-0022](adr/0022-a-driver-that-cannot-transact-may-still-hold-a-writer.md).

`mise run faults` simulates a crash at every window the design makes a durability
claim about, then sweeps them at random, checking after every step that no
sequence number was reused and nothing once readable stopped being readable.

There is a web example: `mise run editor` opens two browser windows on two
identities editing one document, converging through a bare repository between
them. Each window holds its own Y.Doc and its own Ed25519 key, signs every update
against the record it will be stored under, and never shows the key to the server
that stores it. There is a button that types random characters for you, which is
the quickest way to watch concurrent edits converge and the tail grow. See
[examples/yjs/web](../examples/yjs/web).

There is a CLI: `go run -C examples ./cmd/strata` with no arguments prints what it
does. It declares a store's shape once, at `init`, and every verb after that reads
back what the store itself says rather than asserting a shape of its own — an
operator tool has no use case and no business having an opinion about somebody
else's layout.
`strata status` is the one worth knowing — it names the writer holding the
barrier, which is the answer to "why has compaction stopped", and it reports the
unfolded tail against its ceiling. Two ceilings exist and neither has a default,
because a bound nobody chose fires at the wrong moment: `SetCeiling` states the
read cost as a number and refuses writes past it, having warned first;
`SetRefCeiling` states the push cost as a number and only ever reports, since the
remedy is retiring writers and retaining fewer generations rather than blocking
anyone. `strata check`
is the other: it walks every ref and reports which one no longer reads through
to objects this repository holds, which is the failure a crash or a half-fetched
generation leaves behind. `strata verify` is the third, and answers the question
check cannot: whether a generation is the fold it claims to be.

Every maintenance verb prints what it did, how long it took, and — when it did
nothing — the number that explains why:

```
compact  published generation 3 below 192 in 109ms; folded 191 ops into 20 records, 1.4 KiB
compact  nothing to compact in 17ms; the barrier has not reached the next boundary
compact  adopted generation 3 below 192 in 84ms; another clone published it first
prune    dropped 191 folded ops from 200 entries in 166ms
retain   dropped 7 superseded generations in 12ms
compact  published generation 4 below 256 in 96ms; folded 64 ops into 20 records, 1.4 KiB
         erased 3 records; retain, prune and git gc to reclaim the bytes
```

The erasure line prints only when a compaction erased something. A takedown
taking effect is the one line in this output somebody may later have to point at,
and a nightly compaction that erased nothing should not be printing a zero beside
the word.

`SetObserver` is the same information as a struct, for a deployment that wants
metrics rather than a line. The third case above is the one no return value could
express — the fold ran here and was thrown away, which is success, and is also
what a compactor doing nothing useful looks like. Irmin returns the same "fine"
for a collection it performed and one it skipped because another was running, at
a log level below the default, and the consequence is that nobody can say how
often a Tezos node fails to prune.

**The shipped code has no dependencies.** The property suites use
[Hegel](https://github.com/hegeldev/hegel-go), which is a test dependency: a
consumer importing this module builds none of it. That distinction is worth
something only if something enforces it, so the boundary test asserts that no
non-test file imports anything outside the standard library — and that at least
one test file does, since a check that finds nothing is not a check.

Two packages are exempted by name, each for one import and nothing else.
`internal/gitmem` borrows go-git's object encoding, and no consumer can import
it. `project/projecttest` is the generated half of the projection properties,
which an adapter drives from its own tests, and generating them is Hegel's job.
A consumer's test may import it; no shipped file in the library may, so a
consumer that does not reach for it builds no Hegel.

The examples are a module of their own for the same reason, and everything that
binds a domain lives there: the four adapters, the SQLite read model, the CLI and
the yjs editor. A consumer importing the library should never inherit a web
server, a vendored editor or a database driver to get a record store, and their
own `go.mod` is what keeps the question from arising — `go build ./...` here
cannot reach them, and what they require is theirs. `mise run test` runs them
separately, which is also the only place the library gets compiled the way a
consumer compiles it, through a go.mod that merely requires it.

It is not what enforces the two-context split, though it looks it. The examples
require the library, but Go refuses a cycle only between packages, not between
modules: a library go.mod that required the examples could import any adapter
that does not import it back. `examples/boundary` refuses that import, and keeps
the half no import rule can see: that no shipped library file names a product,
and no exported name in the library is a use case's word.

Hegel earns it by shrinking. A hand-rolled loop reports the random 24-op set that
happened to fail; Hegel reports the smallest one that still does, which for the
projection bug above is two facts from one writer differing only in a sequence
number. Its case count is still driven by `-deep`, so the gate has the same knob
it had.

Converting the suites found a hole in one of them straight away. The stamp
generator drew Lamport values from 0..3 — all one hex digit — so
`TestByteOrderEqualsStampOrder`, which exists to pin that the string form is
fixed-width, passed with the zero-padding removed. It draws across hex-digit
boundaries now, and fails as it should.

## A collaboratively edited document

`examples/adapter/doc` is the fourth use case and the one that pushes hardest on what this
design can and cannot do. It keeps the history of a document that several people
edit at once — and it does not merge the document, because nothing here can. Every
merge rule selects a value and none combines two, so a text field written
concurrently by two people would lose one of them. Merging belongs to a sequence
CRDT running above this on its own transport; at ~55ms to commit and ~190ms to
reach another clone, git carries a document's history and has no business carrying
its keystrokes.

What it stores is the CRDT's own update stream, and the fit is closer than it
sounds:

| a CRDT update | an immutable fact |
| --- | --- |
| commutative — order-independent | order-insensitive by construction |
| idempotent — applying twice is a no-op | insert-if-absent |
| carries the client that produced it | keyed by its author, and signed by it |

Storing updates rather than *descriptions of* updates is what keeps attribution
from drifting away from the text. A document is the fold of its updates, so there
are not two accounts of it that can disagree — which an earlier sketch of this,
with signed edit claims beside a separately produced snapshot, could not avoid.

A consolidation is the same idea one level up: the merged state at a version, derived
from the updates and checkable by replaying them. A shortcut, not the data —
exactly what a generation is to a log. Reading a document is *latest consolidation
plus the updates above it*, which is this design's own fold, one level up.

**Provenance of the merged text is available, with a rule the store cannot
enforce.** A CRDT item carries the client that produced it and every item traces
to exactly one update, so replaying only updates signed by known keys leaves a
document in which every character traces back to one. What a signature proves is
who *transmitted* an update, though, not that the items inside carry honest client
ids — nothing stops a signer putting somebody else's id on its items. Closing that
means requiring that items in an update signed by a key carry the client id bound
to that key, which is a check a reader can make and this store cannot: it treats a
payload as opaque, and not interpreting values is exactly what lets it carry them
verbatim.

So provenance is verifiable by a reader that checks the binding — and the binding
is structural rather than a rule anyone has to remember. A client's identity is
*derived* from its signing key, so an update cannot be filed under an identity its
signer does not hold: the record id names the client, a keyring maps that id to
exactly one key, and a signature made by any other key does not verify against it.
`YjsClientID` derives the number to hand `Y.Doc` from the same key, so the id
inside an update agrees with the id it is stored under without this side ever
parsing the payload. What is genuinely unavailable is narrower than it first
appears — and narrower than an earlier draft of this section claimed, which
carried over an objection that applies to positional edit claims ("insert abc at
5", ambiguous once a merge shifts positions) and does not apply to CRDT updates,
which are position-independent by construction.

=== new-region-standup (head) ===
# Runbook: Stand Up a New Prod Region (and its Jurisdiction)

Region-agnostic checklist for bringing up a complete production region:
VPC, databases, the entiredb data cluster, the EKS control cluster, the
regional entire-core, DNS, observability, and the registration that makes the
jurisdiction real. Distilled from three bring-ups — EU (2026-05), AU
(2026-06), IN (2026-07) — and re-checked against the tree on 2026-09-30;
concept background (jurisdiction vs region vs
cluster, per-secret detail) lives in
[eu_entiredb_standup_lessons.md](eu_entiredb_standup_lessons.md).

Worked example: **jurisdiction `in` / region `ap-south-1` / data cluster
`aws-ap-south-1` / control cluster `eks-prod-ap-south-1`** (Mumbai). Every
value below with `in` or `ap-south-1` in it substitutes accordingly.

## 0. Decisions to make first

| Decision | How to decide | IN answer |
|---|---|---|
| Jurisdiction slug | short, DNS-safe (`<jur>.auth.entire.io`) | `in` |
| VPC /16 | next free in the Production /11 (`10.64.0.0/11`) per `docs/vpc-cidr-registry.md` (trust terraform, not the table — fix the registry if they disagree) | `10.74.0.0/16` |
| CockroachDB tier | check the CRDB Cloud console: is the region offered on STANDARD? If not (Sydney wasn't), the regional PII cluster must be ADVANCED — copy `cockroachdb/entire-prod/au` instead of `eu` | STANDARD |
| global-v2 membership | default yes — every prod region carries 3 local global-identity nodes; skipping = novel cross-region identity reads | yes (+3 nodes) |
| App set | which fleet apps run here; EU set (incl. peregrine + himem-xl node group) is the current default | EU set |
| 6 node names | `node-<8 hex>` from uk onward (earlier regions: themed words). AZ placement is by list position for any name that is not literally `node<N>` (aws-cluster `node_az_map`), so append-only edits to the list | placeholders |
| RSL signing generation | prod RSL is bootstrapped, so every new cluster boots with its own signer. Generate a fresh generation 1 for `aws-<region>`, pin `rsl_key_generation = 1` and `ENTIRE_RSL_EXPECTED_SIGNER_KEY_ID` on the cluster unit before its first apply, and review the signer into the fixture with `rsl_signers` and `rsl_coverage_defaults`. The order and the acceptance checks are in [entiredb rsl-new-production-cluster.md](https://github.com/entirehq/entiredb/blob/main/docs/runbooks/rsl-new-production-cluster.md); §3.2, §3.3, §3.4, PR 8 and §6 below carry its steps. Do not leave the pin unset: an unpinned cluster serves with RSL disabled, and adding the pin later needs a node roll. Do not use the bootstrap runbook's steps for one cluster | unset (IN predates the prod bootstrap). `aws-sa-east-1` is the RSL example: generation 1 |
| Shared region list | `aws/regions.hcl` drives Config recording, GuardDuty and Security Hub in every account. A region not already listed is its own PR, applied before anything else — order, access and verification in §0a | already listed |
| Peering mesh headroom | one /16 per region from the Production /11 (28 free), so CIDRs are not the limit. The full-mesh peering is: n regions = n(n-1)/2 peerings, a route per peer in every private route table (default quota 50), and a per-peer entry in every cluster/eks security-group matrix, WARP include and CRDB allowlist. Past ~10 regions raise the route-table quota or move to a transit gateway BEFORE adding the region; below that, copy the next free /16 and close the mesh as in §3.6. CockroachDB caps an ADVANCED cluster at 9 regions through the console (more via the account team), so global-v2 hits its ceiling in the same neighbourhood | 4 regions, no action |
| Turbopuffer region | entire-search vectors stay in-jurisdiction only if Turbopuffer hosts the AWS region (`https://aws-<region>.turbopuffer.com`, list at https://turbopuffer.com/docs/regions). It is serverless: no cluster or namespace to create, the region is just the hostname the cell's indexer and query pods dial (`TURBOPUFFER_REGION` in the fleet search overlays). If the region is NOT offered, decide before the fleet PR whether search runs against another region (vectors leave the jurisdiction) or the cell ships without search (leave the entire-api `SEMANTIC_SEARCH_*` upstream unset) | `aws-ap-south-1` offered |

### 0a. Shared region list: apply order and verification

Adding a region to `aws/regions.hcl` fans Config recording, GuardDuty and
Security Hub into it in every account. Only two region lists in the tree are
guarded by a selftest (`scripts/ecr_lifecycle`, `scripts/app_secrets`); the
rest are kept in step by hand. One PR, nothing CI-applied, in this order:

1. `aws/entire-root/organization`: add the region to `approved_regions` and
   apply from `root-admin`. The DenyUnapprovedRegions SCP on the workload OUs
   otherwise denies every regional write below. entire-root and
   entire-security sit outside those OUs and are unaffected either way.
2. `aws/entire-security/guardduty-detectors`, THEN
   `aws/entire-root/guardduty-delegated-admin`. Delegation enables GuardDuty
   in entire-security for the region, so a detector created the other way
   round fails with "a detector already exists". Recover with
   `terragrunt import 'aws_guardduty_detector.this["<region>"]' '<detector-id>@<region>'`
   (id from `aws guardduty list-detectors --region <region>`; the `@<region>`
   suffix is required with the provider's per-resource region).
3. Every account's `config-recorder` and `account-baseline`: entire-root,
   entire-security, entire-prod, entire-nonprod, entire-backup-prod,
   entire-backup-nonprod, entire-buildkite.
4. entire-root `securityhub-delegated-admin`, `guardduty-detectors`;
   entire-security `guardduty-org-config` (member detectors in the region —
   GuardDuty.1 fires in every member account until this lands),
   `guardduty-notifications`, `guardduty-findings-archive`.
5. `aws/entire-security/securityhub-org-config` LAST. It needs every recorder
   from step 3 live, or the policy association fails in the region and the
   account falls back to Security Hub defaults with every control enabled
   (new-account-standup.md §3).

Access: `security_admin_emails` is deliberately empty, so entire-security
writes assume `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` from `root-admin` — a
`role_arn` + `source_profile` profile, not an SSO tier. `sso-security-readonly`
is read-only.

Expect a burst of elevated alerts in `#alerts-nonproduction` and
`#alerts-production` within a minute of step 5: Security Hub enables itself
in the region and runs the first evaluation on defaults while the policy
lands, so org-disabled controls (Inspector.*) report in every account.
Confirm the association, from entire-security, per account. `--region` is
the Security Hub home region (us-east-2), not the new region:

```sh
AWS_PROFILE=<security-write> aws securityhub get-configuration-policy-association \
  --target '{"AccountId":"<account-id>"}' --region us-east-2
```

`AssociationStatus: SUCCESS` with an `UpdatedAt` at or after the alert
timestamps means the findings came from that window; they archive at the
next evaluation and the alerts resolve themselves. Anything else is the §3
gate: retry with `start-configuration-policy-association` scoped to that
account (new-account-standup.md §3), then re-check.

uk/eu-west-2 (2026-10-01) hit the SCP (#1513 → #1516), the detector order
(#1517) and the alert burst; this section is the record.

### 0b. Day-0 requests (lead time)

File these the day the region is decided, right after the §0a SCP apply —
they have approval lag, and nothing in §3 before the cluster apply needs
them, so they are easy to leave until they block. For a region not yet in
`approved_regions` the quota request itself is denied until that first
apply: `servicequotas` is a regional API and is not on the SCP's exemption
list.

- **EC2 quotas in the new region** (per-region; a fresh region starts at
  AWS defaults). Region-scoped Service Quotas console, "at account level";
  small bumps auto-approve in minutes, larger ones can sit for hours or
  days.
  - EIPs, `L-0263D0A3`, default 5 → request 15+. The network apply takes 3
    (NAT) and clears the default; the cluster apply takes one per node and
    fails at the fourth, tainting the ASGs mid-apply (untaint, don't
    replace — eu_entiredb_standup_lessons.md §1).
  - On-demand Std vCPU, `L-1216C47A`, default 32 → request 192, what the
    existing regions run. Six `*.4xlarge` are 96 and a roll doubles it.
- **CRDB tier**: confirm in the CRDB Cloud console whether the region is
  offered on STANDARD (§0 table); it decides which `cockroachdb/entire-prod/*`
  unit is the template and whether the regional-core DSN needs the fleet
  CA mount.

`examples/yjs` is that division working: a Node client holding the key and the
`Y.Doc`, and a Go bridge that stores, verifies and compacts without ever holding a
key or parsing an update.

```
alice is 86dfb74ec34e7c990e1b
bob   is fc7eb65918f2542f15f2
after compaction: "Hello worldDraft: " from 3 updates
with an unknown client: "Hello worldDraft: " from 3 updates
```

Bob types without having seen Alice and both survive, which is the merge this
store cannot do. The document then rebuilds from what is left after compaction,
pruning and retention, and an update from a client nobody vouches for changes
nothing.

The identity derivations exist twice, in two languages, and drifting apart would
fail silently — updates filed under ids nobody can verify, contributions quietly
absent, no error anywhere. So the Go tests run that client for real and compare
its answers to their own.

## The SQL read model

Git is the source of truth and the transport; a relational database answers the
questions git cannot answer quickly. `examples/project/sqlite` is that read model, and the
reference for what one looks like.

```
records project read.db
```

```sql
SELECT type, id, field, CAST(value AS TEXT), lamport FROM visible;
```

Two tables and a view. `field` holds every value with the stamp that decided it;
`floor` holds each record's delete floor; `visible` joins them, since a
whole-record delete hides fields below it without erasing them and a field written
above it is visible again. The cursor lives in the database and is committed in
the same transaction as the values it accounts for, so it can never run ahead of
them.

**The stamp column is what makes this work.** Every write is a conditional upsert
against it, so the projection is order-insensitive, idempotent and crash-safe, and
can run at the tip of the log rather than waiting for the barrier — a late op with
a lower stamp is refused by exactly the comparison the fold would have applied.
A test asserts that a database built a piece at a time, across compaction and
pruning, is byte-for-byte the database you get by building it from nothing.

**The guard differs by class**, and this is where the read model had a real bug.
"Higher stamp wins" is only the mutable rule: the mirrored class is ordered by
upstream's version token, so a syncer resuming after being offline wrote stale
state with a later stamp and won — the store and the database disagreed about the
current value. The rule is stated once now, as `record.Supersedes`, and translated
into SQL per class. A property test asserts this sink and the in-memory reference
land on the same state for the same ops, drawing from all three classes.

It drives the `sqlite3` binary for the same reason we drive `git`: no
dependencies, no cgo. The cost is a subprocess, so everything batches — a whole
projection pass is one process reading one transaction from a pipe. If `sqlite3`
is not on `PATH`, that package's tests skip and the rest of the module is
unaffected.

## How long until a write is readable

`mise run latency`. Timed end to end — the write is not counted as visible until
the value is readable through the `visible` view a consumer queries, not when
`Apply` returns.

| unfolded tail | commit | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 54.2ms | 18.2ms | 3.5ms | 82.1ms | 88.6ms |
| 200 | 55.7ms | 30.4ms | 3.9ms | 95.7ms | 102.2ms |
| 1,000 | 57.2ms | 78.1ms | 4.4ms | 145.8ms | 150.6ms |

**The database is not the cost.** Writing the batch is 4ms of a 90ms round trip,
flat as the tail grows. What costs is git: one subprocess to commit and several
to read the log back.

**Reading the feed is O(tail), not O(what is new.)** A pass reads every entry in
the unfolded log and then discards what the cursor has already seen, so `feed`
climbs 18ms → 78ms while the work being done stays one op. Pruning is therefore a
read-latency lever and not only a disk one — the tail is what a projector pays for
on every pass, whether or not anything in it is new. A reader that keeps nothing
between passes can pay for only what is new instead: `FeedSince` reads on from
where the last pass stopped, and `FetchFor` fetches no more than that needs
(ADR-0025).

For a reader on another clone, which is what visibility means when git is the
transport:

| commit | push | fetch | feed | apply | total p50 | total p99 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 55.6ms | 61.5ms | 43.8ms | 19.1ms | 3.7ms | 189.8ms | 201.1ms |

Three git round trips and a database write. The two halves belong to different
people: the writer decides when to push, the reader decides how often to fetch.

**Compaction used to spike it, twice over.** Publishing a generation puts the
cursor behind it, so the next pass carries a seed as well as ops. Writing this
gate found two separate reasons that cost more than it should.

The first was not about projection at all: reading a generation walked the shard
tree a level at a time, one subprocess per occupied shard — 141 of them at 200
records, 617ms to read what one recursive listing reads in 5. Every path that
opens a compacted store was paying it. It is one call now.

The second is the seed itself, and the fix is to stop re-reading what the
projection already has. A projection that consumed generation *n* holds everything
in it, so what it needs to reach *n+1* is the difference — and because an
unchanged record encodes to identical bytes and is therefore the same object, git
finds that difference without descending into a shard that did not move. Measured
at the same store state, against the same ops, feeding two cursors that differ
only in the generation they claim:

| records in the store | seed from the diff | seed the whole generation | records seeded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 200 | 43.0ms | 39.6ms | 128 vs 316 |
| 1,000 | 47.2ms | 52.0ms | 128 vs 1,084 |
| 4,000 | 46.5ms | 93.9ms | 128 vs 4,092 |
| 10,000 | 46.8ms | 177.3ms | 128 vs 10,108 |

**The diff is flat and the full seed is linear.** Below about 500 records the diff
is marginally slower — both paths cost the same two subprocesses, and at that size
the bytes are not what is expensive — so the crossover is around a thousand
records and the gap widens from there.

Reading the whole generation is still the right answer whenever this clone cannot
see where the projection was: a projection starting from nothing, or one so far
behind that the generation it last stood at has been retained away. Both fall back
to it, and a test asserts the two paths agree.

**What the store forgets, the projection forgets — but not by applying the
diff's deletions.** A record can leave a generation three ways, and they are not
the same event.

Expiry means the content is gone, and the read model has to follow or it grows
forever with no way to reconcile. It is carried as a Lamport cutoff per Type
rather than a list of what went, because a bare "remove this record" has no
stamp: this feed is unordered and can be redelivered, so an unguarded removal
would delete a value written after it. A cutoff cannot, it is idempotent, and the
full-seed path can state exactly the same cutoff — which is what keeps the two
paths in agreement. In SQL it is one `DELETE` rather than a row per record.

Roll-up is not a deletion at all. It replaces a closed writer's individual facts
with one bundle carrying the same bytes verbatim; nothing is lost, only
re-grained, and the read model keeps the fine grain on purpose. That is what makes
recurrence queries answerable in SQL after the store has coarsened.

Erasure is the third, and it is the one that names its target — which is exactly
what the paragraph above says a projection cannot be handed. It escapes that for
one reason: an erasure carries a **bound**, and a value decided at or above it is
never covered. So re-applying an erasure after the value was rewritten leaves the
new value alone, which is the property the cutoff was invented for, obtained per
target instead of per type. The bound is what makes "remove this record" safe to
say; without it, it is not.

The set is restated on every batch rather than sent once, so a read model that
already held the value when the erasure was written loses it, and a projection
rebuilt from nothing lands in the same place as one that kept up. Both sinks apply
the same predicate — `wire.Erasure.Names` — rather than each forming an opinion
about which rows a target reaches, which is the fix for the bug this seam has
already had once.

## Verifying a generation

A generation is never signed. ADR-0008 rests its trustworthiness on
**recomputation** — anyone can re-derive it and compare — and nothing re-derived
one. `strata check` walks refs for reachability, which answers whether this
repository holds the objects, not whether they are the right objects.

```
verify   generation 5 reproduced from generation 2 and 24 ops
```

**It is inductive, and that is what makes it survive pruning.** Compaction builds
a generation from the one below it plus the ops in between, so verification does
the same: seed from the newest generation below *n* that this clone holds, fold
the interval, compare the bytes. Re-deriving generation *n* from nothing needs
every op below its boundary — precisely the set `prune` destroys once *n* is
published — so on a pruned clone the guarantee the ADR states is unavailable by
construction, and it says so rather than passing:

```
verify   generation 2 is incomplete: the ops it folded are no longer here for J2S6ZP85N1VR4EBSG5HXTD9WBN
```

The generation itself is not pruned, so the next one is checkable against it from
the ops that remain. **A store that compacts and prunes in the ordinary way can
check every generation it publishes, each against the one below.** Skipping costs
nothing either: a generation is defined by its boundary and not by its
predecessor, so any earlier one serves as a base — including generation 0, meaning
nothing, which is the full recomputation. A clone that never held the generations
in between can still check the one it has.

**Four verdicts, because "not reproduced" covers three situations and only one of
them is a finding.** `differs` is the finding. `incomplete` is a clone that cannot
check. `unverifiable` is a build or a configuration that cannot lay that
generation out at all — a newer scheme, or settings this store disagrees with —
and neither of those is a fact about the generation. Collapsing them would make
the verb useless on exactly the clones that most want it, which are the pruned
ones.

**What it folds is what the generation says it folded**, per writer, out of its
own `Folded` map — not everything this clone can see below the boundary. Those are
different sets: a compactor folds what it could see, so a clone that has since
fetched a writer that compactor had never heard of would otherwise report a
perfectly correct generation as wrong, which is the ordinary difference of view
ADR-0010 is about. Selecting the inputs from the description does not make the
check vacuous, because the description is *in* the bytes being checked — a
`Folded` map claiming less than the state holds, or more, lands on different bytes
either way.

**Adoption is where it earns its keep.** A rejected generation push is
arbitration: the loser fetches and takes whatever the remote holds (ADR-0010).
That is the one moment a clone accepts a fold it did not perform — and it then
prunes its own log against that generation's `Folded` map, which is a licence to
destroy ops. So the difference is diagnosed before the ref moves, out of the same
machinery compaction uses when it loses the same race locally, and which the push
path simply never consulted. A scheme, settings or roll-up skew explains two
candidates and is adopted as before for the cost of one blob. What nothing
explains is rebuilt and compared, and a candidate that is not the fold it
describes is refused — which stops this clone publishing until somebody looks,
for the same reason generations are pushed before writer refs.

**The stress suite checks it, which is where it is hardest to hold.** After the
writers stop, every clone verifies every generation it holds (`mise run stress`).
Those runs are concurrent compactors publishing from different views, prunes
racing them, and a remote arbitrating between two candidates for one number — so a
clone is usually verifying a fold it did not perform, which is exactly the case
recomputation exists for. `incomplete` is ordinary there and is not a failure,
since pruning is most of what those runs do; `differs` is the failure and does not
occur.

**The last input a generation did not record was the roll-up set, and writing it
down turned up a data loss.** Roll-up decides bytes — a closed writer's individual
facts become one bundle — and it ran on the writers a compactor could *see*
evicted, which is a view rather than a fact about the fold: two clones that had
fetched different eviction refs folded identical ops into different bytes, and the
divergence they hit reported determinism as broken, which is the third time a
recordable input has surfaced as that accusation. A generation now records the
writers roll-up actually bundled — a function of what was folded rather than of
what was observed, which is the same rule that makes `Folded` safe to record and
membership not — and a skew is `ErrRollUpDiffers`, which the remote arbitrates
like any other.

The loss was underneath it. A closed writer's facts do not have to arrive in one
fold: a boundary falls wherever the barrier let it, so a run's ops straddle one
whenever a lagging writer holds the barrier inside the range that run wrote. The
first generation bundled what was below the boundary; the next fold met the rest
as loose facts under a key that already held a bundle, and seeded a fresh bundle
over the top of it. Every payload the first one carried was gone — silently, since
nothing reads a bundle back to check that it grew, and against the one invariant
this protocol offers a signer, that value bytes are never rewritten however many
generations and roll-ups they have passed through. A bundle is extended now, and
the fold that used to lose it is a test.

## Format versions

Three things get called "the format" and they are versioned differently, which is
deliberate rather than untidy.

**The blob envelope** — `GRC1 | uint16 version | uint8 codec | uint32 len`. An
unknown magic is `ErrNotOurs`, an unknown version is `ErrUnsupported`, and
`wire/testdata/ops-v1.blob` is a frozen corpus a test decodes on every change.
`FormatVersion` is reserved for a change to the framing itself, which has not
happened.

**A payload inside a codec** — versioned by the codec *number*, which is the
mechanism that has actually been used. `CodecGenMeta` (3) → `CodecFoldedGenMeta`
(8) when generations began recording how far each writer was folded;
`CodecBundle` (5) → `CodecStampedBundle` (7) when bundles began carrying the
stamps that let them be expanded back. New number, old number still read for
ever. This is the pattern to reach for: additive, no version bump, nothing
written before stops opening.

**The layout of a generation's record tree** — versioned by a `Scheme` number and
the `Settings` that shape it, both recorded in the generation itself. This one
arrived late: the layout changed three times before anything said so.

The failure that motivated it was not the one you would guess. A full read walks
`state/` recursively and takes each key from the blob rather than the path, so any
layout opens and the fold that builds the next generation is correct whatever
wrote the last one. The hole was in *narrow* reads, which compute a path and ask
for that subtree — and an absent subtree is legitimate, since it is what a type
nobody wrote under looks like. So the read succeeded, returned less than was
there, and looked like an answer. `LoadPartition` against an older generation
returned an empty document.

A narrow read of a generation this build cannot address now reads the whole thing
and keeps what was asked for: correct and slower, which is the right way round
for a read. Compaction refuses to build on a generation from a newer scheme, and
refuses a settings change once with the difference named — `AdoptSettings` says it
was meant. And `genlayout.Scheme` is pinned by a golden test, because a
hand-maintained counter is a thing people forget and this one was forgotten three
times before it existed.

**A structural upgrade is one-way, and both builds coexist for everything but
compaction.** An old clone keeps reading, writing, syncing and — the one that
matters — pruning, because pruning checks `meta.Folded` and never touches a path,
so a clone waiting to be upgraded does not accumulate an unbounded log. What it
loses is compaction, from the moment the first upgraded clone publishes a
generation at the new scheme. That first compaction commits the store: if the
clone that did it goes away, nothing left can compact until another is upgraded.

The generation description is therefore built to grow by **appending fields**
rather than by taking a new codec number. `loadGeneration` reads the meta first,
so a meta an old build cannot decode is a generation it cannot read *at all* —
where a scheme it does not recognise only makes it slower. Locking a clone out of
its own data is a worse outcome than locking it out of compaction, and it is the
outcome strictness buys. A reader that runs out of payload stops and leaves the
rest at zero, and zero already means "read the whole generation".

See [ADR-0013](adr/0013-a-generation-records-what-shaped-it.md).

## Limits

- **Erasure is unreadable at once and unrecoverable on a schedule you run.**
  These are two claims and only the first is immediate. From the moment an
  erasure reaches a clone, no read there returns those bytes — every read applies
  the set, whatever it was narrowed to. Getting them out of storage takes four
  more things: a generation published without them, `retain` dropping the
  generations that had them, `prune` rotating the log ref that carried the op, and
  `git gc --prune=now` on every clone **and on the remote** — manual there,
  because this project requires `receive.autogc` off and a bare remote therefore
  reclaims nothing on its own. Pruning needs the barrier, so a stalled writer
  delays the second claim and `evict` is the escape hatch. `strata status` says
  how far this clone has got and deliberately says nothing about any other: a
  store cannot know what another has retained, because membership is not recorded
  (ADR-0009). A compactor that has not fetched can also publish a generation
  number that was already retained away. That brings back whatever it holds
  until the next `retain` on any clone drops it again (ADR-0026).

  Four things it does not do. A clone offline longer than the erasure window
  never learns the erasure and keeps the bytes — the same qualifier convergence
  already carries, and the right place for this to be bounded rather than a
  separate weakness. An erasure that a losing compactor applied regresses for one
  round, until the next compaction applies it again; reads do not regress. A value
  written above the bound is untouched, because you cannot erase the future. And
  an erasure **names** its target, so an identifier that is itself personal data
  outlives the content it erased — where that is the problem, the answer is the
  layout, one store per subject, and deleting the store is deleting a repository.

  A one-shot writer may not erase, because its log is built to be deleted and an
  erasure is the one thing here with no second copy anywhere. Retiring an evicted
  writer deletes a log too, but it does not refuse: the operator restates that
  log's undischarged erasures in their own first, then deletes. An erasure carries
  its own bound, so restating it is the same statement rather than a new one.

  Any writer may erase anything. An erasure rides a writer's own log, so a policy
  that trusts a writer trusts its erasures; making it an operator-only verb would
  need the receiving hook to see inside a push rather than at the refs it names,
  which is not the shape ADR-0012 chose. See
  [ADR-0017](adr/0017-an-erasure-names-what-may-not-be-read.md).
- **Announcing to a store requires connectivity**, and `Announce` is where it
  happens. A writer announces a low-water mark — a promise never to emit below a
  Lamport value — and the barrier is a minimum over those promises, so
  announcing from a view that has not been refreshed promises something already
  false: the low-water mark lands below a boundary that is folded, and the ops
  that follow are in no generation. Pruning then destroys them, and the barrier
  check does not stop it, because the barrier recovers the moment the newcomer
  catches up. So announcing fetches first, and pushes the announcement before
  returning — one nobody else can see is the same hazard by another route.
  Everything after that point is offline. A store with no remote needs no
  announcement, and a clone that only reads must not announce: an announced
  writer that never writes holds the barrier where it stood.
- **An absent writer stalls compaction**, and that stall *is* the offline-writer
  guarantee — the store refuses to fold a range that writer might still write
  into, so a clone that returns after a long absence loses nothing it wrote while
  away. `Evict` is the release valve, and it is deliberately manual: it trades
  the guarantee away, so only an operator knows whether the writer is really
  gone. Eviction is terminal for that identity; announcing again means a new
  clone, and the writer is told rather than allowed to write into a folded range.
- **Authorization is only as good as the server, and signing is only as good as
  key distribution.** Git has no per-ref authorization, so write access to the
  repository is push access to every store in it unless a server refuses. The
  `pre-receive` hook here is that refusal, and it needs a deployment that
  authenticates: on a path remote there is nothing to authenticate against, so the
  hermetic tests prove the hook and not the perimeter. Record signing is built
  (`examples/adapter/signing`, used by ci and doc) and survives compaction by design, but it has no
  key distribution, rotation, revocation or threshold — a verifier is handed a
  keyring and has no way to learn that a key was withdrawn. gittuf has all four
  and is the obvious place to take them from; its reference-state log is the part
  that cannot come with them.
- **History past a boundary is one revision per generation.** A generation
  records what was current at its boundary, not how it got there, so writes
  between two boundaries collapse once the log holding them is pruned. Good enough
  to show somebody yesterday's version, not an audit log: a value that existed for
  a second can be gone with nothing to say it was there. Retention bounds how far
  back it goes at all. A generation laid out under different settings is read
  whole rather than addressed, so the history is complete but that generation
  costs a full read.
- **Convergence is bounded by the retention window.** Not "will be" — expiry is
  built, so "this store always converges" is already false wherever a type has a
  window set, and the qualifier is part of the contract rather than a future one.
  A peer offline past the window never learns the facts that expired while it was
  away.
- **One shard level holds to roughly a million records.** A generation shards
  record blobs one level deep on `sha256(type\0id)`, 256 ways. That rewrite cost
  is linear in the store: about 36 bytes of tree per record in a touched shard,
  so a single-record change rewrites ~21 KB at 100k records and ~148 KB at 1M.
  The trigger for a second level is a shard tree past roughly 4,000 entries. It
  is deliberately not there yet — Tezos shipped six levels of the same sharding
  and then removed five of them for a 30% speedup, so depth added before it is
  needed is the documented mistake, not the safe default.
- **We pin the `files` ref backend, and git 3.0 is expected to default to
  reftable.** reftable is much better at reading a large namespace and worse at
  the thing this design is built on: it takes one lock for the whole ref store per
  transaction, so two writers pushing entirely different refs contend and one is
  refused with `cannot lock references`. Ten concurrent writers against a reftable
  remote produce that within seconds — the premise that distinct refs do not
  contend, failing.

  Pinning is therefore deliberate, and it is not the whole answer, because a
  remote somebody else hosts is not ours to pin. Push retries lock contention,
  which is a different thing from a rejection: a non-fast-forward is arbitration
  and the answer is to adopt, while losing a race for the ref store's lock decides
  nothing and the next attempt takes it. With that, the sweep passes against a
  reftable remote as well as a files one.
- **A schema change rebuilds the SQL projection rather than migrating it.** The
  database carries a `user_version`, and a build whose schema differs drops the
  tables and re-seeds from the feed on the next projector pass. That is the path
  [ADR-0007](adr/0007-the-projection-stores-the-deciding-stamp.md) already
  guarantees — a rebuilt projection provably lands where an incremental one
  reached, and it is property-tested — so migrations would be a second route to a
  state a tested one already reaches. The cost is real all the same: the cursor
  goes with the tables, so the pass after an upgrade re-reads the newest
  generation and the tail above it before the read model answers again.
- **git error classification is string matching, and only half of it is provoked.**
  `LC_ALL=C` is pinned on every invocation. A lost compare-and-swap and a refused
  push are provoked against real git and assert the outcome rather than the
  wording. The other two are not: a ref vanishing between advertisement and want
  is a race measured at about one run in thirty, and a remote failing mid-write
  did not reproduce here at all. Those tables are asserted instead — every entry
  classifies as its own kind, and none may be shadowed by another, which is how
  two entries that could never fire were found. It stays fragile across git
  versions, and the fragility is not spread evenly.
- **No adapter has met a real upstream.** All three merge classes have adapters
  and are exercised end to end, but the forge adapter has only ever been handed
  entities by a test — nothing here has spoken to GitHub or Linear.
- **No merge that combines contributions.** Every merge rule selects a value;
  none computes one. Counters, add-and-remove sets and collaborative text are
  therefore not expressible as a mutable field — two concurrent increments merge
  to one. The fact class is the substitute (one fact per contribution, aggregated
  in the projection), and the deliberate trade is in
  [ADR-0011](adr/0011-we-merge-by-total-order-not-by-ancestor.md).
- **Compaction has a fixed cost** and is not worth running on a store that has
  barely been written; see the crossover above.

# activity context

Domain language for activity — the two per-jurisdiction services
(`user-activity`, `repo-activity`) that serve residency-safe activity reads.
This file records terms specific to this system so reviews and refactors share
one vocabulary; general programming concepts don't belong here.

## Language

### Authorization

**Authn / authz**:
Authenti*cation* (authn) answers "who is the caller?" — `requireAuth` verifying the
bearer JWT against Core JWKS, producing the **Identity**. Authori*zation* (authz)
answers "may this caller read this scope?" — the **access gate** over the
**AccessChecker**. Authn runs upstream and authz consumes its result; the two never
merge. The httpapi filename `authz.go` holds the gate; authn lives in `router.go`
(`requireAuth`) and the `auth` package.
_Avoid_: using "auth" unqualified for either; filing authz under "authn".

**Access gate**:
The per-request HTTP seam (a Huma operation-middleware) standing in front of the
repo- and project-scoped endpoints. It resolves the caller's **AccessChecker**,
reads the requested scope from the path, and yields a single **fail-closed**
outcome — pass, `403`, `404`, or `503`. Authorizes *before* checking existence
(see below), so the handler body runs only for a caller allowed to read the
scope. Bundled into the `repoOp` / `projectOp` operation constructors, so a route
cannot be registered without its gate.
_Avoid_: auth middleware, authz filter, guard.

**Authz-before-existence**:
The ordering rule the **access gate** enforces — the access decision (`403`/`503`)
is made before any existence check (`404`), so a caller who can't read a repo can
never tell, from the status code, whether it exists in this region. A structural
invariant of the gate, not a per-handler convention.

**Approval gate**:
The waitlist admission check inside `requireAuth`, before the **access gate**
(COR-940). After the bearer verifies, it resolves the caller's live
`accounts.approved` via the **ApprovalChecker** and refuses a waitlisted account
— `403` waitlisted, `503` when the lookup is unavailable (a Core blip is not a
verdict). Admission is per-caller (may this account use the API at all?), not
per-scope like the access gate; the anonymous public-repo flow bypasses it by
construction.
_Avoid_: conflating with the access gate (that's per-repo/project authorization).

**ApprovalChecker** (`internal/auth`):
The process-shared engine behind the **approval gate**: a live Core account read
(the internal-mTLS account-by-id, carrying `approved`) behind a short per-account
TTL cache, with a service-account bypass. Verdicts mirror entire-core's
management-plane gate — waitlisted on a confirmed deny or reaped account,
unavailable (never cached) on a lookup failure.
_Avoid_: treating it as authorization — it gates admission, not scope access.

**AccessChecker** (`internal/auth`):
The per-request authorization decision engine. Wraps the caller's verified
**Identity** with the process-shared **authz.Reader** and caches the caller's
**accessible repo set** for a short TTL. The **access gate** is its HTTP-facing
adapter; the `/me` read path uses it directly as a post-query row filter.
_Avoid_: authorizer, permission service.

**authz.Reader** (`github.com/entirehq/entiredb/modules/authz`):
The read-only client for the **regional read-only SpiceDB**, shared with
entiredb's `core/authz`. It answers `Can`
(point check) and `List` (resource enumeration), derives the subject from the
verified Identity (`authz.AccountSubject(accountID)` — never request input),
maps activity's permission strings to the SpiceDB vocab (repo `pull` →
`authz.Pull`, project `view` → `authz.View`), and fails closed. It holds a gRPC
connection and is a **process singleton** — dialed once at api startup,
shared across every per-request **AccessChecker**. Replaced the old Core
`/access` family.
_Avoid_: SpiceDB client (it's read-only and activity-specific), authz service.

**Accessible repo set**:
The set of repo IDs the caller can currently pull, resolved fail-closed by
bounded point checks (`authz.Reader.BulkCan` on repo/`pull`) over candidates the
caller's own rows or stored preferences name — never by enumerating repo/`pull`,
whose `account:*` public wildcard makes a reverse walk return every public repo
on the cell (COR-1369). The unit of truth for both the gate's repo decision and
the `/me` row filter.

**Fail-closed**:
The posture every authorization path takes: any error reaching the
**regional read-only SpiceDB** surfaces as a denial (`503`), never as
silently-empty or stale-but-allowed-on-error data. The error guarantee is
absolute; **visibility** of grants is **bounded-stale**, not instantaneous (see
**Bounded staleness**) — so a *revoked* grant stops being honored within that
window, not the instant it is revoked.
_Avoid_: fail-safe, fail-open.

**Bounded staleness**:
The consistency model the **authz.Reader** reads under. Checks use SpiceDB's
`minimize_latency` against the regional read replica, so an *allow* decision can
reflect a grant slightly behind the writer — bounded by the replica's
replication lag. To avoid wrongly denying a freshly-granted caller, `Can`
re-checks a *deny* at `fully_consistent` before returning it; `List` (used only
for the membership enumeration) is `minimize_latency` only (stale-tolerant). The
error path stays **fail-closed**; only the allow path tolerates bounded
staleness.
_Avoid_: "strongly consistent", "real-time revocation".

**Stale-denial-OK**:
The per-check opt-out from that deny recheck (`authz.PermissionCheck`), carried by
**read filters** and nothing else. Note what the recheck can and cannot do: it only
ever turns a *denial* into an allow, so waiving it delays visibility of a **fresh
grant** and changes nothing about revocation, which is bounded-stale in both cases.
It is waived where a wrong denial is invisible and self-correcting — a row omitted
from a list (`activityAccessSet`, except a repo the caller named), a response flag
whose consumers re-check before serving data (`ResolveRepoAccess`). It is **kept**
by every gate, and by the one destructive path: `/preferences/repos` re-asks a
denial at full consistency before pruning the stored preference, because that
`DELETE` is not self-correcting.
_Avoid_: calling this "eventually consistent authz" — the *error* posture is still
absolute, and only the deny direction is relaxed.

# Historical control-plane architecture notebook

> **Historical context, not a current runtime or production-readiness guide.**
> This document records the design explored by the original
> `alex/control-plane-prototype`. Many decisions have since shipped, changed, or
> been superseded. Start with `core/README.md`, `docs/auth.md`, current source and
> tests, and focused records in `docs/adrs/`; use this notebook only to understand
> the original design space.

## TLDR

The control plane (entire-core) handles identity, authentication, authorization, and resource lifecycle. entiredb becomes a pure git storage engine that verifies JWTs and checks permissions — it doesn't manage users, orgs, or access control. PII is stored regionally; global services only see UUIDs and public provider identities.

## Context

The auth prototype explored how identity, authorization, and resource management fit together across regional boundaries. Several architectural decisions emerged from building and testing the prototype.

## Decisions

### System boundary: entiredb vs entire-core

**entiredb** is the data plane — git object storage, refs, replication. It has no concept of users, orgs, or permissions. It verifies JWTs via JWKS and calls SpiceDB for permission checks. That's it.

**entire-core** is everything else. It has five subdomains:

| Subdomain | Where | Description |
|---|---|---|
| **Identity** | Global | Accounts (UUID), handles (provider→UUID mapping), public profile cache |
| **Profile** | Regional | Private profile (email), identity audit events (login, IP). PII stays here. |
| **AuthN** | Global | JWT signing keys, JWKS endpoint, login flow orchestration, token minting |
| **AuthZ** | Global | SpiceDB schema, permission checks, relation tuples. **Record-keeper, not decision-maker.** |
| **Control Plane** | Global | Orgs, projects, repos, memberships, grants — the business model. **The authority.** |

### AuthZ is a record-keeper, Control Plane is the authority

**AuthZ** stores relationships and answers permission questions. It doesn't initiate actions or own lifecycle. When asked "can user X push to repo Y?", it walks the SpiceDB graph and returns yes/no. It maintains its own projection of the domain model (repos belong to projects, projects belong to orgs) — just enough to express the permission graph, not to manage the resources.

**Control Plane** (currently `core/resource/`) is the authority for business objects. It decides what gets created, who gets access, and what the rules are. It tells authz to record relations and tells entiredb to create storage. Nothing exists until the control plane says so.

The flow for "create repo":
```
Control Plane: validate request, check permissions
  → AuthZ: write relation tuples (repo→project, permissions)
  → entiredb: init git storage
  → Control Plane: record the resource, return to caller
```

AuthZ doesn't need to know what a "repo" is beyond what the SpiceDB schema defines. The control plane knows the full business model.

**API is a layer, not a subdomain.** Each subdomain can expose its own API surface (HTTP, gRPC, internal). The current `core/api` package is a single HTTP API that cuts across all subdomains — fine for the prototype, but in production each subdomain could have its own API boundary.

### Deployment topology

The subdomains map to deployment units along the PII boundary:

```
Global (deployed anywhere):
  identity, authn, authz, resource
  SpiceDB (stateless, backed by CockroachDB)

Regional (per-jurisdiction):
  profile (one instance per jurisdiction)
  Login flow orchestrator (runs in user's region)
```

The global subdomains never see PII. The regional `profile` subdomain stores PII keyed by UUID. The login flow orchestrator runs regionally because it handles the GitHub OAuth exchange (which returns PII) and needs to route it to the local profile store before calling global.

### PII boundary

PII never reaches the global identity service. The login flow splits the identity provider's response:

- **PublicIdentity** (global): provider, login, provider ID — the identity mapping
- **PrivateContext** (regional): email, IP — stored only in the user's home jurisdiction
- **PublicProfile** (global, cached): display name, avatar — public provider data treated as a cache

The `LoginFlow` orchestrator runs in the user's region. Only `PublicIdentity` crosses the wire to global.

**Transient processing**: The server handling the GitHub OAuth exchange inevitably sees PII in memory (to determine the home region). This is disclosed and minimized — PII is routed to the correct regional store and not persisted locally.

### Two kinds of audit events

- **Domain events** (global): `account:UUID did action on resource:UUID`. No PII. Operation log for the control plane. Can be replicated anywhere.
- **Identity events** (regional): `account:UUID from IP at time`. Login, logout, profile changes. PII stays in the user's home jurisdiction.

The prototype currently mixes these in one regional `audit_entries` table. Production should split them.

### Login flow and regional routing

1. User hits a login endpoint (any region can handle it)
2. GitHub device flow authenticates the user
3. Server gets the GitHub profile (including PII)
4. For new users: home region determined by IP geolocation (overridable)
5. PII routed to home region for storage
6. Global gets only the handle→UUID mapping
7. JWT minted (contains UUID + handle, no PII)

**Returning users**: `ResolveHandle` hits global, returns UUID. No writes to global needed. PII (audit event) goes to home region. JWT minted.

**Cross-region login**: User's home region handles auth. If a US endpoint receives an EU user, it redirects to the EU auth endpoint (like Posthog). The JWT works globally — verified via JWKS.

### Authorization model (SpiceDB)

Zanzibar-style permission checks via SpiceDB backed by CockroachDB:

- **Resources**: org, project, repo, team — with hierarchical permissions
- **Permission cascade**: org owner → project manage → repo push/pull
- **SpiceDB is stateless**: deploys anywhere, reads from CockroachDB, scales horizontally
- **AuthZ is a record-keeper**: stores relation tuples and answers permission questions. Does not initiate actions or own lifecycle. Maintains its own projection of the domain model — just enough for the permission graph.
- **SpiceDB is an implementation detail**: No external system calls SpiceDB directly. The authz subdomain exposes a thin API (`Can(token, permission, resource)`) that handles JWT extraction, resource mapping, consistency strategy, and SpiceDB translation internally. If SpiceDB is swapped for something else, only the authz subdomain changes. entiredb and the control plane call the authz API, not SpiceDB.
- **Consistency**: `FullyConsistent` for permission checks after writes. ZedTokens (see below) for read-your-writes consistency across replicas.

### Resource lifecycle and consistency

The control plane owns business object lifecycle. Creating a resource involves multiple systems that can't share a transaction:

```
1. Control plane: write intent (status: PENDING)
2. entiredb: create storage (entiredb owns repo IDs)
3. Control plane: write authz tuples to SpiceDB
4. Control plane: update status → ACTIVE
```

Permission checks return false until step 3 — SpiceDB has no tuples, so the default is deny. If step 3 fails, the resource exists in storage but is inaccessible. A reconciler retries incomplete intents.

The control plane generates the resource UUID and writes a creation intent *before* calling entiredb. This avoids orphan detection — incomplete intents are the retry queue.

### ZedTokens and consistency

SpiceDB returns a ZedToken (consistency marker) on every write. The token represents "the state of the world after this write." Passing it on subsequent reads guarantees "at least as fresh as this write" without the cost of `FullyConsistent`.

ZedTokens prevent stale reads across SpiceDB replicas. Without them, a user granted access in one region might be denied in another until replication catches up.

ZedTokens don't belong in the JWT — they represent a point in time (the write), not a session. The control plane should capture them on authz writes and pass them to the enforcement point. In practice, CockroachDB replication is sub-second, so the window for stale reads is small. Engineering around it is low priority until measured as a real problem.

### Token architecture

- **Ed25519 signing keys stored in CockroachDB** — prototype expedience only. Private key material in a database is a bad idea for production: compromise of the DB means compromise of all signing keys. Production should use a KMS (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, or similar HSM-backed store) where private keys never leave the hardware boundary. The DB can store key metadata and public keys; signing operations go through the KMS API.
- JWT contains: `sub` (UUID), `handle`, `iss` (entire-core), `kid` (key ID) — no PII, no permissions
- JWKS endpoint at `/.well-known/jwks.json` serves active public keys
- entiredb (and any external consumer) verifies tokens via JWKS — no callback to entire-core needed
- Key rotation: new key created, old keys remain active for verification, deactivation removes from JWKS

### Git operation auth: two token strategies

`git-remote-entire` is the integration point — it runs before every git operation and can handle either strategy. entiredb supports both:

**Thin token (live check):**
```
git-remote-entire → sends JWT to entiredb
entiredb → verifies JWT (JWKS)
        → calls entire-core authz API: Can(token, push, repo:X)
        → entire-core translates to SpiceDB internally
```
Simple. Permissions always current. entiredb never talks to SpiceDB — it calls the authz API which abstracts SpiceDB away.

**Scoped token (no check):**
```
git-remote-entire → calls entire-core: "I want to push repo:X"
entire-core → checks SpiceDB internally → mints short-lived scoped token
git-remote-entire → sends scoped token to entiredb
entiredb → verifies signature + reads claims: {repo:X, push, expires:2min}
```
No authz API call from entiredb. Permissions frozen at mint time but token is short-lived.

**Both (pragmatic path):**
```
git-remote-entire → tries scoped token from entire-core
                  → falls back to plain JWT if entire-core unreachable
entiredb → scoped token? verify and serve
         → plain JWT? call authz API
```

The remote helper already refreshes tokens before each operation. Swapping a token refresh for a scoped token mint is the same pattern, different endpoint. entiredb works either way — scoped tokens are an optimization, not a requirement.

In both paths, entiredb has no dependency on SpiceDB. It depends on entire-core's authz API (for live checks) and JWKS endpoint (for token verification). The authz API is the boundary — SpiceDB is entire-core's internal concern.

### GitHub is the identity provider (for now)

- Handles come from GitHub (`login` field) — we don't manage a global handle namespace
- Device flow for CLI auth (no client secret needed)
- Multiple providers per account supported by the data model (`handles` table with `provider` + `handle` composite key)
- GitHub enforces handle uniqueness within its namespace

### Cross-domain callbacks model service boundaries

Each domain (identity, regional, resource, authz) exposes a Go interface. In the prototype, these are in-process calls. In production, swapping the implementation for an RPC client preserves the same boundary:

- `regional.Service` calls `identity.Service` to verify accounts (callback to global)
- `resource.Service` calls `authz.Service` to write SpiceDB relations
- `LoginFlow` calls both `identity.Service` (global) and `regional.Service` (local)

## Deployment

### Infrastructure

- **EKS cluster** via fleet — entire-core deploys as a fleet app
- **CockroachDB** — existing instances available, no new provisioning needed
- **SpiceDB** — sidecar alongside entire-core pods, or separate deployment. Sidecar is simpler (one pod = one SpiceDB instance, no service mesh), but limits horizontal scaling of SpiceDB independently. Separate deployment lets SpiceDB scale on its own but adds a network hop.

SpiceDB as sidecar makes sense initially — it's stateless (all state in CockroachDB), lightweight, and co-locating it avoids latency on permission checks. Scale it out later if needed.

### Database topology

```
Global CockroachDB cluster
├── database: entirecore
│   ├── accounts, handles, public_profiles, credentials, signing_keys
│   ├── orgs, projects, repos, memberships, permissions
│   ├── domain audit events (no PII — UUID references only)
│   └── goose version tables (per-domain)
│
└── database: spicedb
    └── SpiceDB-managed tables (relation_tuple, etc.)

Regional CockroachDB cluster (one per jurisdiction)
└── database: entirecore_regional
    ├── private_profiles (name, email, bio, company, location)
    └── identity audit events (IP, user agent — PII)
```
